articles.title_orig: Powering China, reshaping Tibet
articles.title_zh: Powering China, reshaping Tibet
articles.content_orig:
To play this audio please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Send a voice message to LivingPlanet
Subscribe to the podcast here via your favorite podcast app: Living Planet Podlink
Lobsang Yangtso: We would just lie down and then, you know, drink directly from the river with your mouth, and then I have this memory because when I turned over that side, you know, I could see a horse drinking at the same time as well. [laughs] Yeah, I mean, I remember that part. Yeah, I mean, you can just you know lie down … and drink directly from the river. You are making me to miss my homeland. [laughs]
For the first twenty years of her life, Lobsang Yangtso lives in eastern Tibet. Then she leaves. Twenty-five years pass before she comes home again.
Lobsang Yangtso: But now, you know, everything has changed.
The Tibet she returns is not the Tibet she remembers.
The no mads gone from the hills where she’d watched them grazing. Instead fences cut across the landscape. CCTV towers overlook villages. And the river from her childhood?
Nobody drinks there anymore, Lobsang says.
But what she's seeing in her hometown is part of something much bigger.
Around the world, countries are racing to cut carbon emissions - and demand is soaring for the resources needed to build a cleaner energy system.
No country is moving faster than China. It leads the world in building solar panels, wind farms, batteries and electric vehicles.
And much of what China needs is found on the Tibetan Plateau: rivers that feed some of Asia’s largest watersheds, along with copper, lithium and other critical minerals.
But this isn’t just a story about energy. It’s about land, culture and power - and who pays the price for progress.
Lobsang Yangtso: my homeland is one of the most beautiful places in Tibet. …
Today Lobsang Yangtso is an environmental researcher for International Tibet Network. As a kid, she ran through fields here, in high-altitude farmland surrounded by mountains. River gorges wind through the region. In the nineties, the mountainsides were dotted with slow-moving yaks, and semi-nomadic herders like Lobsang’s father.
Lobsang Yangtso: "...a few families would take all the yaks from all the households and then they go up on the mountain and then they come back. So it's based on the rotation, and they move from place to place. So it's like a very close way, supporting each other, living together and then especially during summer times, because of the high altitude, we get lots of you know the summer flowers...
Yellow poppies. Purple aster. White wild flowers that she can’t recall the name for.
Lobsang Yangtso: "...and people love to go for picnics, and it becomes community picnics. They love to keep horses in their houses as well. Tibet has lots of glaciers and streams and the small rivers are quite you know common."
In the summer, the river was still cool, fed by snowmelt from soaring mountain peaks. And in the winter, when it froze over...
Lobsang Yangtso: "...then ice skating was quite popular, even though we don't have a you know ice proper ice skating that we see, but … you would see small kids. You know, they have a small wooden chair or something like that, and then your friends pushing you, and then you’re just rowing. We have this belief of believing in the sacred mountain and sacred rivers, and because we believe in deities … we believe that if we exploit or extract any of the resources, or create pollution in that area, because of the deities, you know there is a possibility that you get harmed by that."
Lobsang left Tibet as a teenager. A monk from her village gave his blessing, and she was off to India for university. She didn’t know then that coming home would be so hard.
In the years that followed, the Chinese state imposed more and more restrictions on Tibet.
It took twenty-five years for Lobsang to get a visa to go home. Once she did, she wanted to lay eyes on the monastery she grew up worshipping in.
In the monastery, monks wore the same red robes. Police wore plain clothes.
Lobsang: "Even within the monastery, I could see a police station in the monastery."
Law enforcement had entered the monastery. What had vanished were images of the Dalai Lama, the Buddhist spiritual leader who fled to India in the 1950s, only a few years after Tibet was formally incorporated into the People’s Republic of China.
It was not only the monasteries that had changed. So had the land.
Lobsang: "When I was coming inside from Tendu to my hometown, another really strange thing that I have seen is that the sand mining that they do along the rivers."
Tibetan herders were reporting fish disappearing, and hundreds of yaks dying after drinking polluted water.  Locals said the pollution was a brew of toxic chemicals, leaking from mines upstream. The state is digging for what some call the white gold of the green transition – lithium.
Lobsang: "The river that used to flow in just in front of my house, people don't drink anymore."
Many of Asia’s largest rivers originate in the Tibetan Plateau – that’s why this region is called the "Water Tower of Asia." Downstream, an estimated two billion people rely on the flows that begin in this region.
But it’s not just freshwater that matters here. Today, the Tibetan Plateau is dotted with some of the highest saltwater lakes on Earth. And some of those lakes are reservoirs of liquid treasure: lithium, which we need for the batteries that are so crucial to the clean energy transition.
Meanwhile, locked into the rock of these mountains…
Copper and other materials mined here go into the solar panels that China produces so efficiently.
Some of the largest mines under Chinese state control are in Tibet, pumping out hundreds of thousands of tonnes of copper and other minerals each year.
But the mountains hold another prize for the clean energy transition … gravity.
Ruth Gamble: "The place with the most hydropower potential in Asia– well, actually the world, is the water falling off the sides of the east and the south of the Tibetan Plateau, so that's where the dams have been concentrated in the last-- since the since the end of the Three Gorges Dam in the last 25 years.
My name's Ruth Gamble. I'm the director of La Trobe Asia and a senior lecturer in environmental history at La Trobe University in Melbourne, Australia."
Dams work by storing water… and then letting it drop. The force of that fall turns turbines, and their spinning generates electricity.
Ruth Gamble: "What you have like on the edges of the Tibetan plateau where the water just pachooos down That's a technical term – pachooing [laughs] is where it just charges down off the side of the plateau – it’s the most potential energy, gross potential energy of any water on the planet because the descent is so steep, and the descent is so long, that it can it can create more turning turbines. It will turn more turbines than anywhere else on Earth."
All that falling water makes Tibet one of the most promising places on Earth for hydropower. But…
Ruth Gamble: "Everything else wants to slide down there as well. So landslides and avalanches and outburst floods are all going to come charging down that side of the slope as well."
The advocacy group International Campaign for Tibet counts more than 100 dams planned for Tibet that haven’t broken ground yet. They estimate these projects could displace more than a million people. But, they also estimate these dams would produce enough clean energy to electrify a country with the power footprint of Germany – so projects that could push a million people out of their homes could power tens of millions more with renewable energy.
Ruth Gamble: "It’s not just about whether you transition; it's about how you transition, right?"
China is still the world’s largest carbon emitter, and it’s still building coal plants at a cracking pace. Yet its clean energy buildout is also the fastest in the world, by a wide margin. To wrap our heads aro

articles.title_orig: Mount Dora teacher uses social media wish list to feed hundreds of children
articles.title_zh: Mount Dora teacher uses social media wish list to feed hundreds of children
articles.content_orig:
Lisa Bell , Anchor/Reporter
Robert Breuer , Special Projects Producer
MOUNT DORA, Fla. – Meagan DeWitz may not wear a cape, but the Mount Dora teacher is making a powerful difference for children and families across Central Florida.
“I do this because there are so many children who go to bed hungry and wake up hungry,” DeWitz said.
DeWitz is a full-time third-grade teacher and a mother of two. While working at a Title I school, where most students come from low-income households, she saw that the school’s existing food program could not keep up with the demand.
“God put it on my heart,” she said.
So last August, DeWitz launched an organization called Squirrel Around the World. She began by sharing an Amazon wish list on social media, asking people to donate non-perishable food.
The response quickly grew beyond her expectations. Donations began arriving at her home from people across the country - and even from around the world.
“As soon as it comes in, it’s going out,” Dewitz said. “This is an everyday thing - even on the weekends, even on holidays, and even in the summertime, we’re feeding students and it never stops.”
In less than a year, Squirrel Around the World expanded from serving one school to helping 77 schools and organizations across Central Florida.
The need is often greatest for food that does not require refrigeration, a stove or even a kitchen. DeWitz says some families are experiencing homelessness or living in cars and hotels, making shelf-stable food especially important.
“All of our food is non-perishable,” she said. “It could be eaten right out of the package.”
The work can be overwhelming. DeWitz said she has cried in her driveway and carries stories of the families she helps that she does not always share publicly, but the support from what she calls her “squirrel family” keeps her going.
Sabrina Hutchinson, a third-grade teacher at Seminole Springs Elementary, said DeWitz’s work gives teachers peace of mind.
“Teachers, we tend to worry a lot about our kids when they go home,” Hutchinson said. “We know they’re going home and they’re getting dinner, and they are supported with that.”
Demand remains constant. DeWitz said there are times when the nonprofit’s shelves are nearly empty, but donations often arrive just when they are needed most.
“Last week was one of the slowest weeks of the whole year, and I was stressing out so bad because our shelves were empty,” she said. “Then, at the last minute, my squirrel family said, ‘Meagan, relax. We got this.’”
The shelves were soon filled again.
DeWitz hopes to eventually expand Squirrel Around the World beyond Central Florida and help children in communities around the world. For now, she said the nonprofit’s biggest need is not on her food wish list: warehouse space.
To learn more about Squirrel Around the World or find out how to help, visit the organization’s Facebook or TikTok page and Amazon wish list .

articles.title_orig: Clay Travis: inside the Maga permadad’s world of sports betting, trans panic and more sports betting
articles.title_zh: Clay Travis: inside the Maga permadad’s world of sports betting, trans panic and more sports betting
articles.content_orig:
The rightwing media mogul has lost ground to fellow sports bros like Pat McAfee and Joe Rogan. He’s hoping his new venture can recapture some ground
W hen Maga media blowhard Clay Travis offered $2m to Colin Kaepernick last week to appear on the daily talkshow he hosts with former CIA analyst Buck Sexton, it represented the culmination of a years-long obsession on the right with the onetime NFL star. In Travis’s telling of history, Kaepernick taking a knee during the 2016 NFL season was the event that catalyzed professional sports into the era of “woke” excess from which, he claims, it has been struggling to recover ever since.
But more than simply confirming the right’s longstanding villainization of Kaepernick, Travis’s offer was also a smarmy bid for publicity for his new media venture, Sport & State. Sport & State, which launched in August, is Travis’s bid to get back to his roots as a media mogul who sold the wildly popular Outkick to Fox Sports for a rumored $100m, and reclaim some of the cultural territory lost to fellow sports bros and Magagitators like Pat McAfee, Joe Rogan, Tucker Carlson and Ben Shapiro. But if there’s one thing Sport & State won’t be doing, it’s engaging with anyone beyond the Magaverse. There has been no response from Kaepernick since Travis made his “offer” of $2m to charity in exchange for an interview, which suggests he understands that it was extended more in a spirit of trolling buffoonery than sincerity. No one associated with the left or progressive politics ever appears on Travis’s shows, for the simple reason that they are designed purely for the right to talk to itself. (Some would say the same could be said of the left, although the disregard for dissenting perspectives in the Magasphere seems way more extreme.) More than it heralds a renewal of Travis’s career or an injection of fresh energy into the Trumpist mediasphere, Sport & State is a case study in the stagnation that has taken hold on the right as Donald Trump stares down the barrel of defeat in November’s midterm elections.
Having spent the better part of the past two months listening to the Clay Travis & Buck Sexton Show (which runs from noon to 3pm ET every weekday) and the Clay Travis Show (3-4pm), I can say with confidence that there are, in essence, only 11 topics a given day’s programming on Sport & State will cover: college football gambling picks; Trumpworld figures who are friends with Travis and Sexton; the wonderful job that these figures are doing in power (sometimes mixed with the preceding theme: “Our friend Kash, who is truly our friend, Clay and I are both buddies with him, he’s a good man,” Sexton affirmed on a recent episode); the low levels of testosterone apparently common among white males who voted for Kamala Harris in 2024 (“white dudes for Kamala” is perhaps the gravest slur on the Clay Travis Show); trans women in professional sport (I haven’t calculated this precisely but at a guess I’d say this accounts for 20% to 50% of the discussion on any show that Travis hosts, even as the number of actual trans women competing in professional American sports remains exactly zero and there are probably fewer than 10 trans athletes in total in college sports); crime in America’s cities (in recent weeks the fixation has been Lindsay Clancy , but it’s liable to switch at any moment to Iryna Zarutska, Luigi Mangione, Charlie Kirk, Iryna Zarutska , or whatever murder happens to have taken place on that particular day in New York City); the problem with women (in summary: they are women); the fact that Travis and Sexton are both family men with wives and children; the fact that Travis has a law degree from Vanderbilt University; the fact that Travis studied law at Vanderbilt after he was rejected by Stanford (“I wanted to go to Stanford Law School, they didn’t want me, I went to Vanderbilt instead – I’ve now made a $10m donation to Vanderbilt Law School”); and the fact that Travis appeared on Fox News last night and will appear on Fox News again later today. Sprinkled throughout all of this are plugs for Hard Rock Bet (“Bet $5, get $100 in bonus bets”), which is the official gambling partner of Sport & State and holds equity in Travis’s upstart media concern, and companies such as Perfect 10 Mortgage, Crockett Coffee, XX-XY Athletics and Clay Travis Law, all of which – it should come as no surprise – Travis either outright owns or holds a stake in.
The recursiveness and self-referentiality of the advertising and content on Sport & State are all part of the site’s commercial strategy, according to Travis’s lengthy mission statement . The onshoring of all the advertising will, Travis claims, insulate his new venture from the vagaries of media’s traditional dependence on subscriptions and external advertisers. Gambling is the key revenue driver: Outkick became an affiliate of FanDuel after sports betting was legalized in 2018 and eventually made $350 for every new gambling account it helped set up, netting $2m in affiliate betting revenue on Super Bowl Sunday in 2021 alone, and Sport & State is set up to reap similar rewards through its partnership with Hard Rock Bet. But Travis’s expectation is that his home loan business, say, will also prosper as viewers stay online to hear his views on Ole Miss v LSU, Lane Kiffin or the apparent attempted hijacking of the Israel-bound passenger jet and what it means for the future of DEI in America.
Inadvertently, perhaps, Travis’s sidequest companies offer a sense of what Sport & State’s ideal audience member looks like: a patriotic American male with a habit of deploying the phrase “perfect 10” unironically whose life revolves around mortgages, coffee, litigation, gambling and moaning about trans women. On the Crockett Coffee blog , recent posts include “American Coffee Origins and Brewing Techniques”, “Discovering American Coffee’s Unique Flavors”, and “The Americano: A Complete History” (do I detect a theme here?); Travis sips throughout the day on Sport & State from a black spillproof coffee container, emphasizing his own commitment to the cause of caffeine and country.
If there’s a persistent “ Spider-Men pointing at each other ” quality to the advertising on Sport & State, that extends to the content as well. Travis’s big idea is that in the age of AI and commodified writing, it’s better to go deep than big, that depth of audience commitment matters more than the old traffic era’s scale-focused contest for clicks. There may be some wisdom in the strategy, but that approach – drumming down and appeasing an already loyal base – seems to have become the media-obsessed Trump White House’s guiding political strategy too, a choice that risks self-sabotage as the midterms loom. Travis’s theory of media is second-term Trump’s theory of power: instead of growing the audience, the electorate, the constituency, the sole purpose of having attention is to give those listening more of the same. Discussion on Sport & State this week included a summary of Travis and Sexton’s Monday meeting with Trump in the Oval Office. Their main point was to emphasize that “President Trump says he loves the show, says we’re doing a great job” and that various Trumpworld figures greeted them during their half-hour in front of the Resolute Desk. “We saw Karoline Leavitt, our very good friend”; “We also saw Susie Wiles – she said she is cancer-free now”; “We got a little quick high-five from Stephen Miller”.
Over a chyron announcing THE VOICE OF SEAN HANNITY, the longtime Fox News host then called in to discuss: sports betting (what else?); the border collie he’s about to take delivery of at the conclusion of nine months of dog training (if this is what it takes to survive domestic cohabitation with Hannity as an animal, imagine how things must be for the humans in his house); Gavin Newsom and Kathy Hochul as the highest-taxing, and therefore worst, governors in America; and potential Democratic candidates for 2028 (Hannity thinks A

articles.title_orig: ‘I was fighting for my life’: Indian pilot hailed as hero recalls flydubai cockpit attack
articles.title_zh: ‘I was fighting for my life’: Indian pilot hailed as hero recalls flydubai cockpit attack
articles.content_orig:
Smit Machchhar says in video call with Indian PM that he realised if he did not get up then ‘passengers would lose their lives’
The Indian pilot who helped thwart an apparent attempt to crash a flydubai flight has described how he fought for his life in the minutes after his co-pilot stabbed him and the plane began a steep descent.
Capt Smit Machchhar, who is recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, told the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, in a video call broadcast live on television news channels that he knew he had to get back on his feet to save the passengers onboard.
“I had so many wounds. I had fallen down,” he said on Friday from the hospital, his head bandaged and tubes in his nose, before breaking down as he recalled the attack.
“I was fighting for my life. At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives,” he told Modi.
Machchhar, who is from Mumbai, was seriously injured in Wednesday’s attack but managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter and restrain the attacker as the Boeing 737 descended sharply, witnesses and Israeli authorities said. He has been hailed as a hero for his actions, with world leaders saying he helped prevent a potential disaster.
The flight, carrying 182 people from Dubai to Tel Aviv, was diverted to Tabuk in north-western Saudi Arabia for an emergency landing.
The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said the attacker, an Omani national, was arrested in Saudi Arabia and was undergoing interrogation there. His motive for the attack remains unclear.
Machchhar said that during the difficult moments, he recited the Hanuman Chalisa, a devotional hymn dedicated to the Hindu deity Hanuman and traditionally recited as a prayer for strength and courage.
“Lord Hanuman gave me courage,” he told Modi.
Machchhar, who is married and has two children, has worked for flydubai for about four years, according to his LinkedIn profile. Before joining the airline, he spent 11 years with SpiceJet, an Indian low-cost carrier, where he served as a senior commander and line training captain. He logged more than 9,750 flying hours with SpiceJet.

articles.title_orig: Preserving human rights heritage for future generations in Chile
articles.title_zh: Preserving human rights heritage for future generations in Chile
articles.content_orig:
An agreement with the Museum of Memory to preserve archives of the Evangelical Lutheran Church in Chile documenting the church’s defense of human rights during the country’s military dictatorship.
Evangelical Lutheran Church in Chile Bishop Izani Bruch (left) with representatives of the Museum of Memory and Human Rights during her visit to the national institution. Photo: IELCH
(LWI) - The Evangelical Lutheran Church in Chile (Iglesia Evangélica Luterana en Chile -IELCH) has signed a collaboration agreement with the country’s Museum of Memory and Human Rights ( MMDH ) to preserve and highlight documents that bear witness to the church’s social action and work in the defense of fundamental rights during the country’s military dictatorship.
Following the agreement, the Lutheran church will donate to the museum various documentary collections relating to its work during that period. These documents will be digitized and incorporated into the historical heritage safeguarded by the MMDH, a national institution, based in the capital, Santiago de Chile.
In the background, hundreds of photographs of people detained and disappeared during Chile’s last military dictatorship can be seen. Photo: IELCH
The agreement will help to preserve artefacts, documents and testimonies relating to IELCH’s work in the defense of human rights. Photo: IELCH
Evangelical Lutheran Church in Chile Bishop Izani Bruch alongside representatives of the Museum of Memory and Human Rights examining historical documents at the national institution during her visit there. Photo: IELCH
The documents that the church is entrusting for preservation — pastoral letters, reports, records of accompaniment, denunciations, minutes of community work and testimonies from persecuted people— constitute a spiritual and ethical heritage that bears witness to the prophetic diakonia exercised by the church during a time marked by death, torture, suffering, enforced silence and the systematic violation of fundamental rights, noted IELCH Bishop Izani Bruch.
The signing took place following the bishop’s visit to the museum in August. During the occasion, she lit a candle in memory of Herbit Ríos Soto, the son of Yolanda Soto, a member of the IELCH La Paz congregation, who was detained and disappeared. Some of the archives and historical objects preserved by the museum include the typewriter of Lutheran Bishop Helmut Frenz, who was actively involved in the defense of human rights until he was barred from returning to Chile following a trip to Germany.
During the difficult period of Chile’s 1973 - 1990 dictatorship, the IELCH provided pastoral accompaniment to victims and their families, denounced abuses, and provided open spaces for refuge and promoting justice, Bruch explained. “This prophetic diakonia was neither partisan nor ideological: it was a faithful expression of our Lutheran confession, which recognizes that faith is lived out in history and that love of neighbor requires us to defend people’s lives, dignity, freedom and integrity,” she emphasized.
Preserving these documents at the Museum of Memory means ensuring [...] that new generations — in Chile and around the world — will be able to learn how a small, but deeply committed church became a place of ethical resistance, a space of consolation and a prophetic voice in the face of injustice.
Bishop Izani Bruch, Evangelical Lutheran Church in Chile
“Preserving these documents at the Museum of Memory means ensuring that this testimony is not lost, distorted or relegated to oblivion. It also means that new generations —in Chile and around the world — will be able to learn how a small, but deeply committed church became a place of ethical resistance, a space of consolation and a prophetic voice in the face of injustice,” Bruch emphasized.
The agreement also represents recognition of the church’s public witness and commitment to those who suffered persecution and repression during one of the most difficult periods in Chile’s recent history, Bruch said. It is “an act of faithfulness to the gospel, service to the country and a contribution to building a collective memory that can help us move toward a more just, more aware and more humane society.” She concluded: “Memory is part of the church’s mission: remembering in order to heal, remembering in order to learn, remembering so that violations of human rights and human dignity may never again be repeated in our country.”
Representatives from the Museum of Memory and Human Rights alongside Evangelical Lutheran Church in Chile Bishop Izani Bruch. Photo: IELCH
Visiting various significant areas of the museum. Photo: IELCH
While ensuring the preservation of a significant part of the IELCH’s institutional memory in the MMDH, the agreement will facilitate access to these materials for education, reflection, and the promotion of human rights. The church will also receive support for the preservation of its own collections, including minutes, photographs and documents, as well as digitized copies that will remain in the church’s institutional archives.
LWF Regional Secretary for Latin America and the Caribbean and North America Rev. Sonia Skupch highlighted the agreement’s significance for the Lutheran communion. “One of LWF’s core values is dignity and justice, by which we acknowledge that all people are created in God’s image and are therefore dignified in God’s eyes, and that their human rights are inalienable,” she said.
The torture and deaths that occurred during the dictatorship in Chile must never happen again. Acts of remembrance are part of the journey toward achieving a more just society that can live in peace.

articles.title_orig: ‘I couldn’t let everybody else die,’ says hero Flydubai pilot Smit Machchhar
articles.title_zh: ‘I couldn’t let everybody else die,’ says hero Flydubai pilot Smit Machchhar
articles.content_orig:
Smit Machchhar, the hero Flydubai captain who fought off a savage attack by his copilot , kept fighting because he could not “let everybody else die,” he said in his first public remarks since Wednesday’s suspected hijacking attempt.
“In that moment, I was fighting for my life,” Machchhar told India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi in a video call on Friday. “I was so severely wounded that I had fallen down… at that time, I was thinking what if I don’t get up?”
A horrific mid-air catastrophe on flight FZ 1073 heading to Tel Aviv was averted in a stunning turn of events on Wednesday when passengers bravely rushed into the cockpit and stand-in pilots regained control of the aircraft.
Machchhar was badly injured while trying to fend off the attacker. Images showed a gruesome scene onboard, with blood splashed across the cockpit and the seriously wounded pilot lying on the floor, his pained face partially covered with a mask.
Machchhar told Modi he was on the ground in the cockpit when he realized the plane was going down.
“And I knew in that moment – one last push, Smit! Just do it. The door is right there,” he said. “And even at that time, he was beating me up.”
“And then I just opened it… and then everybody came,” he said, referring to several other passengers who then rushed into the cockpit and restrained his attacker.
“I was doing this for my life, but at the same time, I knew that I couldn’t let everybody else die.”
Modi praised Machchhar’s heroics, telling the veteran pilot that his “courage, patience and quick thinking… saved the lives of so many people.”
“You yourself were fighting the battle of life and death,” Modi said.
Machchhar is recovering at a hospital in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates (UAE). He was initially treated for his injuries in Saudi Arabia, where the diverted plane was forced to make an emergency landing.
The father of two had suffered “massive blood loss” and was “severely wounded,” dentist Shota Musaev, a passenger on the flight who helped treat him, previously told CNN.
His bravery “managed to prevent a 9/11 disaster,” Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told CNN on Wednesday.
Captain Smit Machchhar: The ‘jovial’ pilot and father who thwarted the Flydubai attacker
Machchhar appeared emotional in the call with Modi while recalling the ordeal, and apologized to the prime minister for crying on the phone.
The two later spoke in Gujarati, the language predominantly spoken by people from India’s western state of Gujarat, which is where Modi is from.
Machchhar said his daughter had come to visit him in hospital but got scared seeing him in his condition. His youngest son, who is two, has not been able to meet him yet, he said.
Born into a family in the textile business, becoming a pilot wasn’t Machchhar’s “childhood dream,” he told the Bona-Fide Banter podcast in 2025. Initially, he’d enrolled in a textile engineering course after school.
Speaking to Modi, Machchhar said he felt a sense of pride.
“Now that you have called me, I am really really proud of myself,” Machchhar said. “I wasn’t proud before this, but now I am.”
The plane’s co-pilot and Machchhar’s alleged attacker has now been transferred from Saudi Arabia, where the plane landed, to the UAE, where he faces a terrorism investigation.
He is an Omani national, Netanyahu told CNN Thursday. Oman and Israel do not have formal diplomatic relations, and it is not yet clear how the Omani pilot would have obtained clearance to fly to Israel.
Authorities are yet to divulge the co-pilot’s identity. And there hasn’t been any confirmation of his motive or of the weapon he used in the violent altercation, though Netanyahu suggested to Fox News this might have been a knife or an axe.
The Israeli prime minister said the suspect had undergone “Islamist radical indoctrination,” adding that it was too early to say whether he had connections to Iran or anyone else.
Netanyahu said the attacker was suicidal, adding that he had called out “kill me” after being restrained by other passengers.
US President Donald Trump suggested later Thursday the pilot may be linked to Iran , though he provided no details.
This story had been updated with additional details.

articles.title_orig: El Al forced to cancel first rescue flights to Dubai after authorities revoke landing permissions
articles.title_zh: El Al forced to cancel first rescue flights to Dubai after authorities revoke landing permissions
articles.content_orig:
El Al Israel Airlines has been forced to cancel its rescue flights to Dubai , the company announced on Friday morning, after Israeli airlines' permission to land there was revoked by the authorities.
El Al stated that, as soon as official permission is granted for the rescue flights to resume, it would be implementing the planned flights to bring stranded Israelis home.
Meanwhile, the Transportation Ministry said that "following coordination with all relevant parties, it was agreed that flights operated by Israeli airlines from Dubai to Israel would begin on Friday, October 2. However, due to the need to complete the necessary preparations and coordination by security officials for the operation of the flights, a delay is expected in the departure of the repatriation flights from Dubai.
“Citizens currently in Dubai should remain in contact with the airlines through which their tickets were booked and follow their instructions and updates,” the ministry added.
According to estimates, more than 10,000 Israelis are stranded in Dubai and at other destinations from which they had been expected to return to Israel via the United Arab Emirates .
Later on Friday, Israir announced that it had received the final approvals from the Emirati authorities and that flights would be departing from Israel to Dubai during the day. No similar announcement was made by El Al.
On Wednesday, a flydubai aircraft that departed Dubai for Tel Aviv was diverted and landed in Saudi Arabia following an altercation between the captain and the copilot.
During the incident, one of them was stabbed, prompting the activation of the distress signal.
The aircraft initially disappeared from flight tracking systems, raising concerns that it had been hijacked . However, after several tense moments, the circumstances surrounding the incident became clearer, and the plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

articles.title_orig: Old combines and corn pickers from around the world
articles.title_zh: Old combines and corn pickers from around the world
articles.content_orig:
This slideshow of 14 pre-1986 harvest machines, submitted by readers, spans more than a century of harvest seasons.
We asked, and our readers delivered.
A couple of months ago, we asked our readers to send us their photos of old combines and corn pickers — anything pre-dating 1986 — whether they were running through the fields or parked permanently in a grove of trees. And our readers came through in a big way, not only from Nebraska, but also from across the country and around the world.
John Joe Lyons sent us photos of his 1980 S1540 New Holland combine in the field harvesting winter barley in Ireland. Martin Cleveland sent us a vintage shot of a 1938 Minneapolis Moline Twin City MTA tractor pulling an MM combine, with Cleveland’s father, Erik, of the Kelley, Iowa, area, operating the machine.
And Ken Yoder of Sudlersville, Md., sent a nice photo of his 1978 John Deere 7700 combine harvesting soybeans on what is called Delmarva Peninsula on the Eastern Shore of Maryland.
We’ve gathered more than 100 reader photos of their experienced combines and pickers, going back to the turn of the last century through 1986. We can’t show you every single photo emailed to us, but we’ve compiled scores of photos covering more than a century of harvests to share with our readers — thanks to our readers.
Related: What to know before buying an on-farm semitruck
We are sharing a slideshow here of a few of those harvest machines, and we will continue to work through our substantial collection of photos over the coming months, sharing with you online photo galleries you can click through into 2027.
Some of the photos are in color; many are in black and white. Some are a little blurry, a little dark or, perhaps, there was grain dust on the camera lens. But just the same, they all represent memorable moments from harvest seasons years ago, and the farmers who worked in those fields.
Sit back and click through our first slideshow of those great combines, corn pickers and threshing machines that we all love, going back more than 100 years from around the globe.
senior editor of Nebraska Farmer, Nebraska Farmer
Curt Arens began writing about Nebraska’s farm families when he was in high school. Before joining Farm Progress first as a field editor in 2010, and then as editor of Nebraska Farmer in 2021, he had worked as a freelance farm writer for 27 years for newspapers and farm magazines, including Nebraska Farmer. His real full-time career during this period was farming his family’s fourth-generation land near Crofton, Neb., where his family raised corn, soybeans, wheat, oats, alfalfa, cattle, hogs and Christmas trees.
Curt and his wife, Donna, have four children: Lauren, Taylor, Zachary and Benjamin. They are active in their church and St. Rose School in Crofton, where Donna teaches. The family now rents out their crop ground to a neighbor, but still lives on the same farm first operated by Curt's great-grandparents. The family runs a few cows and other assorted 4-H and FFA critters.
Previously, the 1986 University of Nebraska animal science graduate wrote a weekly rural life column, developed a farm radio program and wrote books about farm life. He received media honors from the Nebraska Forest Service, Center for Rural Affairs, Nebraska Association of County Extension Boards and Nebraska Association of Natural Resources Districts.
He wrote about the spiritual side of farming in his 2008 book, Down to Earth: Celebrating a Blessed Life on the Land , garnering a Catholic Press Association award.

articles.title_orig: Uzbekistan dominates chess Olympiad while England’s Sivanandan, 11, sets new world age record
articles.title_zh: Uzbekistan dominates chess Olympiad while England’s Sivanandan, 11, sets new world age record
articles.content_orig:
Host nation won having led almost from start to finish, while young English player reached a stunning landmark
Uzbekistan, the host nation, won the open gold medals at the 2026 Olympiad, the biennial chess international team tournament, at Samarkand last week in the style of the legendary Soviet grandmasters of long ago. India, the defending champions, were second, Germany a surprise third, and the top-seeded United States fourth.
The hosts led almost from start to finish, with world No 5 Nodirbek Abdusattorov and the world title challenger Javokhir Sindarov their top-board powerhouses. The team recovered swiftly from a single defeat by Germany, and were particularly impressive in crushing Armenia by 3.5-0.5 in the penultimate round. The Uzbekistan government rewarded each of the five players with $200,000 (£178,000), plus $50,000 for the coach Rustam Kasimdzhanov.
India performed in line with their seeding. Putting the world champion, Gukesh Dommaraju, on board four boosted his results but also underlined that Sindarov is the favourite for the coming world championship match. Gukesh was exposed in the final rounds when he was outplayed against both Germany, although he won that game fortuitously, and Hungary.
The final leading scores were: Uzbekistan 20/22 match points; India and Germany 18 ; USA, Azerbaijan, Armenia and Hungary 17 ; China, France, Spain, Ukraine and England 16 (206 teams competed).
England’s creditable 12th place, one below their seeding, would have been still higher if a third player had performed at the level of the nine-time British champion Michael Adams, 54, and the Spectator chess columnist Luke McShane, 42, who were both in contention for individual medals right up to the final round. England’s women were 15th against their seeding of 20th, and the combined performance was the best since at least 2018, and probably since 1990.
Russia/USSR, which monopolised Olympiad golds in the second half of the 20th century, have been banned from the last three competitions due to the invasion of Ukraine. If allowed to take part, a team of Ian Nepomniachtchi, Andrey Esipenko, Daniil Dubov, Vladislav Artemiev and Alexander Grischuk would have been contenders.
The potential of Turkey’s Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus stands out. The 15-year-old won the individual silver medal unbeaten and has advanced to No 17 in the live ratings, a similar level to Bobby Fischer at that age and well ahead of current world No 1 Carlsen when he was 15. Here he defeats a rival prodigy , Argentina’s Faustino Oro.
China won the women’s Olympiad ahead of Kazakhstan, India and the US, and did so with its B team. World champion Ju Wenjun, world No 1 Hou Yifan, former title challenger Tan Zhongyi and world No 3 Lei Tingjie all stayed at home, but their substitutes, led by world No 4 Zhu Jiner and 16-year-old Lu Miaoyi, proved highly effective.
For the future, the US is potentially a powerhouse in women’s chess. Its duo of Carissa Yip, 23, and Alice Lee, 16, are both targeting the open GM title and its $100,000 bonus offered by Dr Jeanne Cairns Sinquefield, while new candidates are emerging in Rachael Li, Rose Atwell and Zoey Tang who are all teenagers with 2300+ ratings.
Bodhana Sivanandan broke the world age record for the youngest ever woman grandmaster (WGM). Her 8/11 total, playing all games with no rest days, included six wins, draws against Ukraine’s reigning European champion Anastasiia Hnatyshyn and Georgia’s former World Blitz champion Nana Dzagnidze, both of them current world top 20 players, and a solitary loss to Deysi Cori of Peru due to a time-pressure blunder in a drawn ending.
The 11-year-old Harrow schoolgirl’s record as the youngest ever WGM broke Hou’s 2006 mark by several months, and she also recorded her second norm (of three needed) for the international master (IM) title at open level. For IM, she also needs a 2400 rating against her current 2382, which includes the Olympiad.
Her last-round Olympiad game was a model of what has become her trademark style of a Magnus Carlsen grind.
If she secures her final norm and becomes an IM before her 12th birthday, she will break the all-time female No 1 Judit Polgar’s world age record and also become one of the 10 youngest ever IMs. She is already No 2 among all players born in 2015, behind only Russia’s IM Roman Shogdzhiev, who has been groomed for several years as a potential heir to Anatoly Karpov.
after newsletter promotion
The Guardian’s Matthew Weaver interviewed Sivanandan after her return home. At the end of the Olympiad the youngster talked with Lichess.org’s Theo Wait , while chess.com also covered her achievements in detail .
The Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport’s new £250,000 a year Supporting Elite Chess Fund document contains no specific provision for rewarding world-record breakers. Maybe it should, as Sivanandan’s IM title and new record could follow as soon as the London Classic, which begins in November.
Sivanandan has just started at secondary school, and that could slow her progress on the chessboard. The advance from IM to GM is difficult, and many talents eventually plateau, which should temper extrapolations of a rise comparable to Polgar and Hou.
Meanwhile Timur Turlov, 38, a Russian-born entrepreneur from Kazakhstan whose company Freedom Holding has a multibillion dollar valuation on the Nasdaq index, was elected as the new president of the world chess body Fide last Saturday.
The previous Fide President, Russia’s Arkady Dvorkovich, had planned to run for a third term but was forced to withdraw due to EU sanctions on his assets and travel visas.
Turlov received 96 votes against 76 for the German businessman Wadim Rosenstein and a surprisingly low 20 for the ticket of Jan Henric Buettner of Freestyle Chess and the ECF’s international director Malcolm Pein. In the run-off ballot they switched to Turlov, who defeated Rosenstein 110-85.
Turlov is young, committed and with proven business skills. However, there could be an immediate problem since Rosenstein has appealed to the court of arbitration for sport over the new president’s eligibility.

articles.title_orig: DOJ charges Boston man with threatening conservative podcaster Katie Miller
articles.title_zh: DOJ charges Boston man with threatening conservative podcaster Katie Miller
articles.content_orig:
The FBI on Thursday arrested a man on a charge of stalking former Trump administration adviser Katie Miller, an administration official familiar with the investigation told NBC News.
John Anthony Proia III, 41, was arrested and charged with stalking over allegations that he called, texted and left voicemails with “disturbing messages” about the victim, who was described as a former political adviser, and her husband, who is currently a high-level federal government employee, the Justice Department said in a news release.
The Justice Department did not name Katie Miller, though an administration official familiar with the investigation confirmed to NBC News that the victim is Miller, who is married to White House deputy chief of staff for policy Stephen Miller and hosts a popular conservative podcast.
“Thank you Todd Blanche, Leah Foley, and the FBI Washington Field Office for keeping me and my family safe. Good to see a Boston grand jury indict this man,” Miller wrote Thursday on X , referring to Attorney General Todd Blanche and U.S. Attorney Leah Foley.
Proia was indicted by a federal grand jury in Boston on Thursday on one count of cyberstalking after being arrested earlier in the day. He is alleged to have contacted the former political adviser more than 40 times in less than two months, according to the Justice Department.
The defendant is also accused of sending disturbing messages to Miller’s parents during the August-to-September time frame cited in court documents.
“As alleged in the Indictment, the defendant repeatedly and relentlessly targeted the victim, her husband and her family with deeply disturbing communications that profoundly disrupted their lives,” Foley said in a statement.
Ted Docks, special agent in charge of the FBI’s Boston Division, wrote in a statement on Thursday that Proia was arrested “for allegedly engaging in a sustained campaign of harassment to frighten this victim and her family, inflicting significant emotional distress.”
Proia made the calls, sent text messages and left voicemails from “an ever-changing series of unfamiliar phone numbers” to Miller, who lives in the Washington, D.C., area, the DOJ said.
The department added that those phone numbers were obtained through applications that provide free phone numbers for calling and messaging via Voice over Internet Protocol. The applications allow a user to hide their identity and easily generate new phone numbers, according to court filings.
According to court documents, Miller sometimes received multiple communications from Proia in one day, including calls made late at night. Miller did answer some of the calls, but Proia also left voicemails, the DOJ said.
The calls “were allegedly made by what appeared to be a male caller employing a menacing tone and often using expletives,” the Justice Department said.
The Justice Department also detailed some text messages sent to phone numbers associated with Miller’s parents.
One message Proia is alleged to have written to Miller’s mother called Stephen Miller “evil” and Katie Miller a “creature.” Another message was said to feature a photo of Katie Miller, while another read, “My god, how can you be proud of this filth?”
In a text message to the victim’s father, Proia is alleged to have written, “Hey [first name of victim’s father], how goes it? Hope your daughter marrying a Jewish Nazi/white supremacist is working out for you and [first name of victim’s mother]. Did you raise her to be trash or did that just happen naturally?”
Proia’s arrest comes after Bloomberg reported over the weekend that two senior FBI officials in Washington were demoted and reassigned to FBI headquarters due to concerns that the agency was not moving efficiently enough to investigate threatening phone calls made to Miller, three people familiar with the matter told Bloomberg.
Darren Cox, assistant director in charge the FBI’s Washington Field Office, told Bloomberg in a statement that the move was a personnel decision made at the field office level based on “our constant evaluation of mission needs.”
Michael Kosnar is the Justice Department Producer for NBC News.
Kyla Guilfoil is a breaking news reporter on the politics team for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: S&P 500 futures edge higher as September jobs report looms: Live updates
articles.title_zh: S&P 500 futures edge higher as September jobs report looms: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Stock futures inched higher early Friday as traders awaited the release of September's jobs report.
S&P 500 futures were up 0.5%, while futures tied to Dow Jones Industrial Average were up 276 points, or 0.5%. Nasdaq-100 futures advanced 0.8%.
In the regular trading day, the Dow and the Nasdaq Composite ended the session marginally higher. The S&P 500 posted a 0.2% advance to conclude the first trading day in October. All three indices are on pace for weekly losses, with the Dow off 1.7% in the period.
Treasury yields climbed to multiyear highs before retreating. The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield soared to 5.344%, its highest level since 2002. The yield on the 30-year Treasury bond also reached its highest in 24 years.
Yields continued to pull back early Friday, trading marginally lower in the early hours of the morning.
It came as oil prices fell sharply on reports that the U.K. and Europe were considering a release of strategic fuel reserves. The Trump administration has pressured European allies to "immediately" release diesel supplies.
Front-month Brent crude oil futures were last seen 2.2% lower at $100.05 per barrel, after dipping below the $100 mark earlier in the day. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude oil futures were down by 3.2% to $89.85 a barrel.
Despite volatility in the markets, Luca Paolini, chief strategist at Pictet Asset Management, said he expects global stocks to "power on" thanks to strong earnings momentum.
"After a nine-month rally in equity markets and a recent spike in bond yields, stocks appear expensive relative to fixed income," he said in a Friday morning note. "However, we believe earnings growth remains a more powerful market driver. Companies in the MSCI World index are on track to deliver earnings growth of more than 30% this year, while emerging market firms could see profits rise by over 65%."
September's nonfarm payrolls report will also be in the spotlight Friday, with the Dow Jones consensus calling for job growth of 84,000 and for the unemployment to hold steady at 4.1%.
The report comes as traders reassess the next move for the Federal Reserve. Fed funds futures trading suggests a 72% likelihood the central bank will stand pat in October.
Given that the current narrative suggests the labor market is stable, a strong jobs report alone would likely not push the Fed to hike in October, said Christopher Hodge, a chief U.S. economist at Natixis CIB Americas. Hodge expects growth in the manufacturing and construction sector amid a data center buildout.
"We expect payrolls to slow from the torrid pace from August, but still to register solid gains. We expect payrolls to increase by 60k, which if realized, would bring the three-month moving average of gains to 81k," Hodge said.
Asian stocks closed mixed on Friday. Japan's Nikkei 225 lost 0.94%, while South Korea's Kospi added 0.46%. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 traded 0.79% higher. Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was 2.8% lower in its last hour of trade. Mainland China markets were closed for a holiday.
European stocks were broadly higher, with the regional Stoxx 600 index rising by almost 1% in early trading.
Moderna will replace Warner Bros. Discovery in the tech-heavy blue-chip Nasdaq 100 index after the biotech's shares have risen nearly sixfold over the past year.
The change will take effect before the market opens on Oct. 9, the stock exchange said in a statement late Thursday.
Shares of Moderna rose 2.4% in premarket trading, adding to a 563% gain over the past 12 months.
The company, which became a household name after it developed one of the first vaccines for Covid-19, surprised the Street last month when an experimental personalized cancer vaccine co-developed with Merck showed positive initial results in its first-ever late-stage trial.
Meanwhile, Warner Bros. is in the process of merging with Paramount Skydance . Paramount has said the merger will close on Oct. 6.
European government bond yields fell on Friday, as they headed for the end of a volatile week that saw yields on various regional securities hit multi-decade highs.
By 9:15 a.m. in London (4:15 a.m. ET), yields on British and German 10-year government bonds were around 7 basis points lower. Their Italian counterparts saw yields move 4 basis points lower, while 10-year bonds issued by France and Switzerland saw yields fall by 2 basis points.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 added 0.3% in early morning trading, with tech stocks leading gains.
Germany's DAX index, up 0.3%, led gains among major regional bourses.
Asian stocks closed mixed on Friday. Japan's Nikkei 225 lost 0.94% to 68,309.46, while the Topix closed 0.99% lower at 4,091.
South Korea's Kospi rose 0.46% to 7,003.74, while the small-cap Kosdaq slid 0.11% to 893.29.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 added 0.79% to 8,682.1.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was 2.8% lower in its last hour of trade.
Mainland China markets were closed for a holiday.
Volvo Cars shares are down by more than 5% in premarket trading after the Swedish automaker flagged an increasingly challenging market situation and deteriorating near term outlook, which have hit cash flow and sales volumes.
The group told investors it would not fulfil its previous full-year outlook statements, with lower-than-expected sales and a weaker full year outlook for the company.
"The decline is primarily driven by further deteriorating market conditions in China and slower than expected recovery in the US, while Europe remains resilient," Volvo said.
Brazilians vote on Oct. 4 in the first round of a closely watched presidential election, with incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro dominating the polls.
The result could influence Brazil's relationships with the U.S. and China, including over trade and access to critical minerals, as Bolsonaro emphasizes alignment with Washington while Lula stresses Brazilian sovereignty.
Approximately $1.1 million of the nearly $388 million stolen from crypto exchange Bitget in last week's cyberattack has been frozen, as the platform continues efforts to trace and recover the assets.
Frozen assets had not necessarily been returned to the exchange, CEO Gracy Chen told CNBC in an email interview. She did not disclose how much had been recovered.
Speaking on CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Wednesday, Chen said she was "not expecting to recover a lot of funds," citing the limited recovery from previous cryptocurrency exchange hacks. However, "exchanges have a responsibility to demonstrate how they protect users, particularly when something goes wrong," she said.
U.S. Treasury yields rose on Friday, reversing some of the previous session's declines as longer-dated borrowing costs remained near multi-decade highs.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield climbed 1.8 basis points to 5.252%, while the 30-year Treasury yield rose 2.6 basis points to 5.629%.
Treasury yields had eased Thursday after their recent surge, with investors continuing to weigh the outlook for the U.S.-Iran conflict and its potential implications for inflation and interest rates. Yields move inversely to prices.
The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission has proposed new rules that would make it easier for investment advisers and regulated funds to hold cryptocurrencies on behalf of clients, as U.S. regulators push ahead with writing crypto rules after a sweeping legislation stalled in Congress.
The proposal, announced Thursday stateside, would establish a tailored framework governing how registered investment advisers, investment companies and business development companies hold custody of crypto assets.
The changes are aimed at modernizing decades-old custody requirements and removing regulatory barriers that the SEC says have limited advisers' ability to offer crypto-related investments.

Fresh policy support, falling stocks and rising demand for Chinese bonds shape the week’s market narrative
A sell-off in technology stocks pushed mainland Chinese equities to their lowest level in more than a year, even as Beijing stepped up support for the economy with a key interest rate cut. At the same time, Chinese government bonds attracted fresh interest as US Treasury yields climbed to a new high.
Here are some figures that have captured market attention this week.
Mainland China’s CSI 300 Index dropped 2.2 per cent on Monday to its lowest level since August 21 last year, while the technology-focused Star Market 50 index tumbled 4.1 per cent. A 31 per cent plunge in the Star Market 50 during the third quarter contributed to a 12 per cent decline in the CSI 300.
Mainland Chinese and Hong Kong stocks could face a bumpy road in the fourth quarter amid underwhelming stimulus measures, concerns over further interest rate increases and changing sentiment towards artificial intelligence-related investments, analysts said.
China’s central bank cut the one-year pledged supplementary lending rate to 1.5 per cent from 1.75 per cent on Tuesday, aiming to encourage policy banks to provide funding for projects aligned with national priorities.
The move came alongside a mortgage interest subsidy programme for first-time homebuyers, offering an annualised interest subsidy of 1 percentage point for up to five years for loans with principals of up to 1 million yuan (US$149,000).

articles.title_orig: OpenAI fires 3 safety researchers accused of sharing confidential company information: report
articles.title_zh: OpenAI fires 3 safety researchers accused of sharing confidential company information: report
articles.content_orig:
Fortescue executive chairman and founder Andrew Forrest discusses the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence on 'Barron's Roundtable.'
Three researchers have been fired from OpenAI after allegedly sharing confidential company information with a third-party AI safety organization, sources told The Wall Street Journal.
The three researchers worked on the company's safety team, the Journal reported.
"We have parted ways with three individuals for violating our policies on accessing and handling sensitive company information," an OpenAI spokesperson told the outlet.
"Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work," the spokesperson added.
TRUMP SIGNS EXECUTIVE ORDER REBRANDING AI AS 'SUPER INTELLIGENCE' AS TECH TITANS INK SEPARATE SI ACCORD
The firings come amid heightened scrutiny of AI safety as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has publicly warned about the need to keep increasingly powerful artificial intelligence under human control. (Reuters/Manuel Orbegozo / Reuters Photos)
The firings come as OpenAI and several other major artificial intelligence companies have disclosed incidents involving AI models engaging in unexpected behavior or autonomously accessing other companies' systems.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced last week that an OpenAI agent gained unauthorized access to an Australian government website earlier this year.
The company said there was no evidence that patient records were accessed.
In July, OpenAI disclosed that one of its advanced AI models autonomously hacked into the infrastructure of another AI company, Hugging Face, during internal testing in what it described as an "unprecedented cyber incident ."
Last week, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned the United Nations Security Council that rapidly advancing AI could threaten humanity if governments and industry fail to keep it under human control.
MIKE ROWE WARNS US WORKFORCE FACING ‘PROBLEM OF THE DECADE’
OpenAI said it parted ways with three employees for violating company policies governing access to and handling of sensitive information. (Reuters/Dado Ruvic/Illustration / Reuters Photos)
OpenAI has also released information outlining six instances in which its models engaged in what the company described as misaligned behavior.
The company said it found examples of its AI models creating self-generated instructions, concealing mistakes in task summaries, fabricating information using exposed API keys, uploading files to the internet in order to cite them and engaging in unsanctioned communication and collaboration between agents.
CLICK HERE TO GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO
Headquarters of artificial intelligence company OpenAI with elevated glass skybridge and blue abstract sculpture on a sunny day, San Francisco, California, August 14, 2025. (Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images / Getty Images)
FOX Business confirmed earlier this week that OpenAI safety leaders made the decision not to release its new AI model, GPT-6.1 Astra, due to safety concerns.
"For anything regarding safety and alignment, there’s a trade off. You really do need to find what’s the right line between staying within scope, but also avoiding laziness in terms of how the model actually pursues tasks even when it hits friction," Saachi Jain, OpenAI's head of safety systems, said in a statement.
"While [GPT-6.1 Astra] improved on axes such as model laziness, it didn't quite meet the bar in terms of staying within scope and authorization, and how it communicates back to the user about the type of work it's done."
FOX Business has reached out to OpenAI for comment.
FOX Business' Sophia Compton contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Not-so-brave new world: virtual taekwondo makes Asian Games debut
articles.title_zh: Not-so-brave new world: virtual taekwondo makes Asian Games debut
articles.content_orig:
Kazakhstan's Rita Bakisheva (R) competes against India's Kashish Malik in the mixed individual virtual taekwondo
Taekwondo dates back more than 2,000 years, but on Friday at the Asian Games the Korean martial art stepped into a not-so-brave future where nobody gets hurt: virtual taekwondo.
At a gymnasium about a 90-minute drive from the main Games host city of Nagoya, a modest number of spectators watched with a mix of fascination and bewilderment.
Taekwondo officials have billed it as "real-world martial arts meets cutting-edge virtual technology".
Competitors wear a VR headset and motion tracking technology allows their movements to control their in-game avatars.
They have "nodes" on their back, thighs and shins to pick up each bodily action.
Rounds are typically 60 seconds each and matches are a best of three rounds, the two combatants standing within their own play area a few metres apart.
The goal is to aim real-life kicks to the virtual body and head of their opponent to deplete their computerised health bar.
The opponent is physically there, standing on an opposing side, but there is never any real-life contact.
Darren Yap won bronze -- to go with another bronze in the traditional format.
"It was fun playing out there. I had zero expectations," said the Singaporean.
Asked what he could see through the VR headset, he said: "You can see your health bar, your opponent's character, your limbs.
"It's actually quite nice to wear.
"It's a fun way to do sparring and it's a fun way to do taekwondo without the contact."
Officials say virtual taekwondo is just as athletically demanding as the real thing, but safer.
Governing body World Taekwondo "proudly endorses" it, calling it "groundbreaking".
Sceptics say it is just another type of gaming.
The first world championships were in 2024 in Singapore, but on Friday it arrived at a bigger stage.
One of the differences to the real-life sport is that men and women compete in a mixed category. There are also no weight classes.
"It allows more people to participate in the sport, and I think it's cool that women are able to beat men," said Yap, 22, after losing his semi-final to Vietnam's woman athlete Chau Ngoc Tuyet Sang.
Singapore has become the early home of the sport. Virtual taekwondo appeared at the inaugural Olympic Esports Week in the city-state in 2023.
Silver medallist Chau, who also competes in the real-life format, had mixed feelings about no gender or weight separation.
"One advantage is that you don't have to worry about the difference in weight," the 21-year-old said.
"But one disadvantage is that men and women can have differences in physical strength, and men may tend to be stronger.
"That could also mean that some of the movements are faster than those performed by women."

articles.title_orig: Falcon Heavy flies its first mission for U.S. spy satellite agency
articles.title_zh: Falcon Heavy flies its first mission for U.S. spy satellite agency
articles.content_orig:
Update Oct. 1, 12:21 a.m. EDT (0421 UTC): SpaceX landed its two side boosters.
A SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket launched from Florida Thursday night on a classified mission for the National Reconnaissance Office, America’s spy satellite agency.
Codenamed NROL-97, the mission blasted off from Launch Complex 39A at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center at 11:54 p.m. EDT (0354 UTC). It took a north-easterly trajectory on departure from Florida’s Space Coast.
The NRO has previously flown payloads on 22 Falcon 9 rockets but this is the first time it has used the heavy-lift Falcon Heavy, which consists of three Falcon 9 boosters and an upper stage, topped by a payload fairing.
The powerful rocket, which lifts off under the power of 27 Merlin 1D engines, was introduced to great fanfare in 2018 and made its 14th flight Thursday night.
Like most NRO missions, little is publicly known about the nature the flight. It was the first NRO mission to fly after being procured in 2025 through the competitive National Security Space Launch (NSSL) Phase 3 Lane 2 contract.
The Falcon Heavy core stage, serial number B1106, was brand new and was expended on this mission. The rocket’s side boosters both flew just a month ago to launch NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. B1104 made its second flight and B1072 was on its fourth mission.
The side boosters returned to Landing Zones 1 and 2 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station with thunderous sonic booms. SpaceX returned LZ-1 to service for this mission after it was replaced by LZ-40 at Space Launch Complex 40. However, that landing pad was used earlier in the day on Thursday by the booster returning from launching the Crew 13 mission, B1101.
The NRO said the payload fairing was previously used on the NROL-95 mission in July.
NROL-97 was SpaceX’s third Falcon launch of the day. In addition to the Crew 13 mission, the company launched 130 payloads on the Transporter 13 rideshare mission from its West Coast pad at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. It was the first time the company has landed four boosters in a single day.
This was the third launch of a GPS satellite in as many years. Liftoff of the GPS 3-9 mission from pad 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station launched at 11:53:16 p.m. EST on Tuesday, Jan. 27 (0453:16 UTC on Jan. 28).
NASA and SpaceX officials briefed the media Wednesday on the planned launch of a Falcon 9 rocket and Dragon cargo capsule on a resupply flight to the International Space Station.
SpaceX and NASA launched a planet-hunting satellite Wednesday from Cape Canaveral, two days after calling off a launch attempt to conduct additional guidance, navigation and control analyses. Liftoff occurred at 6:51 p.m. EDT (2251 GMT), and the first stage of the Falcon 9 rocket successfully landed on a drone ship in the Atlantic Ocean.

articles.title_orig: Trump illegally fired Seattle’s U.S. attorney, judge rules
articles.title_zh: Trump illegally fired Seattle’s U.S. attorney, judge rules
articles.content_orig:
The ruling is the latest in the administration's battle over U.S. attorneys.
A federal judge on Thursday ordered a U.S. attorney from Western Washington who was fired by President Donald Trump in July to immediately be reinstated to the position, and is barring the Justice Department from again attempting to replace him.
The ruling from U.S. District judge Stanley Bastian is the latest escalation in the Trump administration's battle with the judiciary over DOJ efforts to install U.S. attorneys around the country without Senate confirmation.
Federal judges appointed Rogoff to the post that oversees federal prosecutions in Seattle in July, and he was fired by President Trump through an email roughly an hour later.
Rogoff then filed suit citing similar cases around the country where the Trump administration had unsuccessfully sought to install attorneys and extend their service indefinitely, which judges appointed by both parties have ruled clearly violates the appointment statute .
The Justice Department said it disagrees with the decision and plans to appeal and seek a stay.
Judge Bastian ruled from the bench in Thursday's proceeding granting Rogoff's request for a preliminary injunction -- and further enjoined Attorney General Todd Blanche and the Executive Office of the President from taking any further moves to effectuate his termination.

articles.title_orig: Scientists Invent Underwater Umbrellas to Protect Coral Reefs—and It Appears to Be Working
articles.title_zh: Scientists Invent Underwater Umbrellas to Protect Coral Reefs—and It Appears to Be Working
articles.content_orig:
As the climate warms, corals around the world are facing increasingly frequent marine heat waves that lead to widespread coral bleaching. Scientists are racing to protect the world’s reefs with a variety of interventions, such as supplementing reefs with replanted corals, boosting coral immune systems with beneficial microorganisms, and deploying underwater shades to protect them from the Sun’s rays.
A new study published in Frontiers in Marine Science adds to evidence that this shading strategy can prevent—and sometimes reverse—bleaching for two Atlantic coral species. Though scientists have deployed similar shades over Pacific corals , research on shading has been limited in the Atlantic Ocean. The strategy could aid coral restoration and preservation efforts by protecting particularly vulnerable corals in the Caribbean and beyond during marine heat waves.
Corals are animals that get up to 90% of their nutritional needs from so-called symbionts: single-celled photosynthetic algae that live within coral cells. The density of the algae and the amount of chlorophyll they contain determine how light or dark a coral is. When a coral is bleached and its symbionts are gone, “the coral is slowly starving,” said Karen Neely , a marine biologist at Nova Southeastern University in Florida and an author of the new study.
In 2023, one of the Caribbean’s worst marine heat waves led to a widespread bleaching event. In the aftermath, Neely and the research team wanted to see whether shading could help protect coral species in the Atlantic as it has elsewhere in the world.
“As soon as those shades went on, those corals all recovered.”
The team assembled 20 shades made of polyvinyl chloride (PVC) pipe, foam, and agricultural shade cloth. They set the shades over communities of two Atlantic brain coral species, Pseudodiploria clivosa and Colpophyllia natans , at Newfound Harbor, a protected reef in the Florida Keys . The shades remained in place between August and November 2024. During that time, the researchers monitored the corals’ color and sampled the symbiont community.
Researchers measured the extent of bleaching by matching the color of the coral to colors on the Coral Health Chart , a tool created by a research nonprofit at the University of Queensland in Australia. They compared their findings with measurements taken from nearby corals that had not been shaded.
During the study, sea surface temperatures at Newfound Harbor breached the Florida Keys’ bleaching threshold of 30.5°C (86.9°F) for at least 61 days—conditions at which corals start to become stressed. In 2024, the reef faced the second-highest cumulative heat stress on record, according to NOAA.
Shaded corals showed less bleaching overall, and some even recovered from bleaching that had occurred earlier in the season—showing that interventions can still help after a bleaching event has already started. “We weren’t able to get the shades out until the corals had already started paling in color, and so we weren’t sure if this was going to be too late to have any sort of impact,” Neely said. “But what we found was that as soon as those shades went on, those corals all recovered.”
Mark Warner , a marine ecological physiologist at the University of Delaware who was not involved in the new study, said the results weren’t surprising and that scientists have observed that cloudy days and large storms can mitigate bleaching events.
The research team had also expected the species composition of algal cells within a coral to change depending on whether the corals were shaded or not. However, the species of symbionts and the rate at which the amount of symbionts changed were roughly the same across all corals, shaded and unshaded. Neely said this result could be because all the symbionts were already heat tolerant following the 2023 marine heat wave, which may have wiped out symbiont species that weren’t. “They were already as heat tolerant as they could be,” she said.
Still, the fact that both the paler, unshaded corals and darker, shaded corals had similar algal densities could mean the corals weren’t bleaching in the traditional sense, in which algae leave their coral hosts, Warner said. “Even their control corals, which paled as the temperature was rising…really weren’t losing their symbiotic algae any faster than the treatment corals.”
It’s possible that the algae within the unshaded corals were acclimating to high amounts of sunlight by decreasing their amount of chlorophyll, Warner said, which would have changed the pigment of the coral rather than the amount of algae. However, he noted, the research team was limited by their sampling—permitting restrictions meant the team could sample only the algal community present at the edges of corals, rather than the tops, which would have faced the Sun.
Researchers hope the study provides environmental managers with evidence that shading can work for Atlantic coral species.
Neely hopes that the study provides environmental managers with evidence that shading can work for Atlantic coral species. “Something being trialed in another part of the world might not make managers as comfortable as something that’s been trialed here on our own reefs and with our own species and shown to be successful,” she said. “That opens up the doors for managers who might want to think about wider implementation.”
“One thing that surprised us was how easy it was [for the shades] to be effective,” Neely said. The research team had anticipated that they’d need to clean the shades regularly or that the equipment might not be durable enough. But the shades stayed relatively clean and low-maintenance. Plus, the shading strategy is about 10 times cheaper than the cost of replacing a dead coral, the authors wrote.
Neely emphasized that the shades are a small-scale solution best for protecting high-priority corals, such as particularly large, rare, or beloved specimens—“corals that managers decide we just can’t afford to lose.”
Neely said that next, she’d like to study how shading affects the long-term health of corals. Even if corals don’t die from bleaching, the slow starvation that bleaching causes can make corals more susceptible to disease and less able to reproduce. Shading coral could preserve its strength for disease resistance and reproduction, she said.
—Grace van Deelen ( @gvd.bsky.social ), Staff Writer
