articles.title_orig: Israel's Netanyahu: Co-pilot of flydubai plane underwent radical Islamist indoctrination
articles.title_zh: Israel's Netanyahu: Co-pilot of flydubai plane underwent radical Islamist indoctrination
articles.content_orig:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says investigations suggest the man who stabbed his fellow pilot and tried to take over a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination".
The Flydubai plane plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) two hours into its journey on Wednesday, before passengers and crew overpowered the attacker and retook control to land safely.
Netanyahu told Fox News that it was looking "very likely" that the attacker, who he said was an Omani national, "was going to down the plane".
Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) state news agency reports investigations have begun there to determine "whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose".
The Interior Ministry of Saudi Arabia - where the plane made an emergency landing - said that both the pilot and co-pilot had been sent back to the UAE on Thursday morning after medical teams had cleared them.
UAE officials earlier claimed jurisdiction over the incident because the aircraft on which the attack took place is registered there and flies under its flag.
Netanyahu told Fox that once the attacker had been subdued and tied up by passengers and crew, he was "calling out to the aircrew 'kill me, kill me', so it's clear he was suicidal - that's not a question".
Passenger Almog Itali said it felt like a "rollercoaster" as Flight FZ1073 fell 17,000ft in less than two minutes
"And with all the passengers in there, and if you couple that with what I just told you about the Islamist tendencies, that radicalisation that were found in his background, I think... that'll give us a pretty good clue."
However, he stressed that he did not want to draw any firm conclusions as to motive yet.
Both US President Donald Trump and UAE officials have indicated to the media that Iran may be responsible for the incident, without definitively blaming Tehran.
Trump told reporters on Thursday that Iran would be "hit very hard" if it was deemed to have been involved in the attack.
Pilots from countries without diplomatic relations with Israel were usually not allowed to fly there, Netanyahu said when asked about how the suspected Omani pilot came to be on the plane.
He added: "Obviously there was a loophole here and we're taking care of that among other things... with the full co-operation, I have to say, of the Emirati government, so we're both interested in making sure this doesn't happen again."
Oman has not formally established official ties with Israel , unlike the UAE.
The prime minister was also asked earlier on the same network whether there was an indication if Iran was involved, he replied: "It's too early to say".
Flydubai passenger describes hugging his children as plane nosedived during attack
Who is the 'hero' Indian pilot who was stabbed on Israel-bound flight?
Both Netanyahu and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said the stabbed pilot, Indian national Capt Smit Machchhar was a "hero".
India's ambassador to the UAE Deepak Mittal visited Captain Machhar in hospital on Thursday, the Indian Mission confirmed on social media, stating he was "in good health and recovering well".
The Indian government has praised Smit Machchhar for his "immense courage"
Preliminary findings from a separate Israeli investigation into the incident, suggest that the alleged attacker intended to crash the plane, an Israeli security source told BBC Arabic.
The source said the investigation - led by Israel's intelligence agency Mossad - interviewed passengers after they arrived in Tel Aviv to establish what had happened on the plane.
Flydubai's flight FZ1073, with more than 170 people on board, took off from Dubai International Airport in the UAE at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time), en route to Ben Gurion Airport.
Two hours later, the 17,000ft drop in altitude was reported on the plane tracking website Flightradar24 and minutes later the plane signalled an emergency code.
At about 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent, landing safely at  Tabuk Airport in the north west of Saudi.
Flydubai has since suspended flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv as it carried out its own investigation into the incident.
Israel's Transportation Ministry said the suspension aligns with Netanyahu's directive.
Israeli airlines including El Al, Israir and Arkia said plans were in place to operate rescue flights from Dubai starting on Friday to bring back stranded passengers.
The Transportation Ministry also said it sent an urgent request to Etihad Airlines to increase the number of flights between Abu Dhabi and Tel Aviv.

articles.title_orig: Massachusetts man accused of cyberstalking campaign against Katie Miller
articles.title_zh: Massachusetts man accused of cyberstalking campaign against Katie Miller
articles.content_orig:
The FBI on Thursday arrested a man on a charge of stalking former Trump administration adviser Katie Miller, an administration official familiar with the investigation told NBC News.
John Anthony Proia III, 41, was arrested and charged with stalking over allegations that he called, texted and left voicemails with “disturbing messages” about the victim, who was described as a former political adviser, and her husband, who is currently a high-level federal government employee, the Justice Department said in a news release.
The Justice Department did not name Katie Miller, though an administration official familiar with the investigation confirmed to NBC News that the victim is Miller, who is married to White House deputy chief of staff for policy Stephen Miller and hosts a popular conservative podcast.
“Thank you Todd Blanche, Leah Foley, and the FBI Washington Field Office for keeping me and my family safe. Good to see a Boston grand jury indict this man,” Miller wrote Thursday on X , referring to Attorney General Todd Blanche and U.S. Attorney Leah Foley.
Proia was indicted by a federal grand jury in Boston on Thursday on one count of cyberstalking after being arrested earlier in the day. He is alleged to have contacted the former political adviser more than 40 times in less than two months, according to the Justice Department.
The defendant is also accused of sending disturbing messages to Miller’s parents during the August-to-September time frame cited in court documents.
“As alleged in the Indictment, the defendant repeatedly and relentlessly targeted the victim, her husband and her family with deeply disturbing communications that profoundly disrupted their lives,” Foley said in a statement.
Ted Docks, special agent in charge of the FBI’s Boston Division, wrote in a statement on Thursday that Proia was arrested “for allegedly engaging in a sustained campaign of harassment to frighten this victim and her family, inflicting significant emotional distress.”
Proia made the calls, sent text messages and left voicemails from “an ever-changing series of unfamiliar phone numbers” to Miller, who lives in the Washington, D.C., area, the DOJ said.
The department added that those phone numbers were obtained through applications that provide free phone numbers for calling and messaging via Voice over Internet Protocol. The applications allow a user to hide their identity and easily generate new phone numbers, according to court filings.
According to court documents, Miller sometimes received multiple communications from Proia in one day, including calls made late at night. Miller did answer some of the calls, but Proia also left voicemails, the DOJ said.
The calls “were allegedly made by what appeared to be a male caller employing a menacing tone and often using expletives,” the Justice Department said.
The Justice Department also detailed some text messages sent to phone numbers associated with Miller’s parents.
One message Proia is alleged to have written to Miller’s mother called Stephen Miller “evil” and Katie Miller a “creature.” Another message was said to feature a photo of Katie Miller, while another read, “My god, how can you be proud of this filth?”
In a text message to the victim’s father, Proia is alleged to have written, “Hey [first name of victim’s father], how goes it? Hope your daughter marrying a Jewish Nazi/white supremacist is working out for you and [first name of victim’s mother]. Did you raise her to be trash or did that just happen naturally?”
Proia’s arrest comes after Bloomberg reported over the weekend that two senior FBI officials in Washington were demoted and reassigned to FBI headquarters due to concerns that the agency was not moving efficiently enough to investigate threatening phone calls made to Miller, three people familiar with the matter told Bloomberg.
Darren Cox, assistant director in charge the FBI’s Washington Field Office, told Bloomberg in a statement that the move was a personnel decision made at the field office level based on “our constant evaluation of mission needs.”
Michael Kosnar is the Justice Department Producer for NBC News.
Kyla Guilfoil is a breaking news reporter on the politics team for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: FIFA World Cup Matches Bring $850 Million to Bay Area, Report Says
articles.title_zh: FIFA World Cup Matches Bring $850 Million to Bay Area, Report Says
articles.content_orig:
The FIFA World Cup generated roughly $850 million in economic impact in the Bay Area, according to a new report released by regional organizers.
The report was unveiled Thursday by the Bay Area Host Committee, a nonprofit formed to bring major sporting events to the region, with a board of directors made up of heads of local professional sports teams, whose venues often host events or play supporting roles.
The estimated figure is based on metrics evaluating spending by visitors, teams and companies on things like hotels, food, transportation and events, and the wages earned by workers in the region related to the World Cup. The report was prepared for the host committee by Boston Consulting Group.
“Hosting FIFA World Cup 2026 elevated our global reputation, strengthened community bonds and will pay dividends for years to come,” Zaileen Janmohamed, the president & CEO of the host committee, said in a statement.
“The world’s attention on our region showcased the Bay Area as a premier destination for major international events, brought neighbors together through watch parties and shared celebration, and will continue to fuel future tourism as visitors who experienced our hospitality choose to return and recommend the Bay to friends and family,” she said.
The report said the lion’s share of the impacts — about $410 million — were seen in Santa Clara County. Levi’s Stadium, in the city of Santa Clara, was designated as the sole venue for all six World Cup matches played in Northern California.
The stadium was stripped of its branding under FIFA rules, and temporarily dubbed San Francisco Bay Area Stadium .
About $240 million of the boost was felt in San Francisco County, and the remaining $200 million was spread among eight other Bay Area counties: Alameda, Contra Costa, Marin, Napa, San Mateo, Santa Cruz, Solano and Sonoma, according to the report.
The matches and supporting events and celebrations supported “approximately 5,100 jobs across the region and drew an estimated 240,000 visitors from outside the Bay Area, underscoring the tournament’s reach across the region’s hospitality, retail and service sectors,” the host committee’s statement said.
The $850 million figure exceeded the committee’s previous projections for economic impact, which the organization pegged at $480 million to $630 million. It attributed the increase to higher-than-anticipated daily visitor spending.
“The world saw what we’ve known all along — the Bay Area is a world-class sports [region] that excels in bringing people together, welcoming fans from around the globe and delivering an extraordinary World Cup experience,” Gov. Gavin Newsom said in a statement.
“This success was a true team effort, and I could not be more excited for the major sports events to come in the Bay Area.”
The combined events of the 2025 NBA All-Star Game at Chase Center in San Francisco, and Super Bowl LX and the World Cup matches at Levi’s Stadium, generated roughly $1.9 billion for the region in total, according to the host committee.
However, the eye-popping totals proffered by organizations like the host committee are frequently called into question by economics experts and academics.
Roger Noll, a professor emeritus of economics at Stanford University, previously characterized the estimates in such reports as “grossly overstated” and said they serve mainly as public relations or advertising to help justify the large logistical lift, interruptions to public life and costs of hosting major events in the region.
The report prepared for the Super Bowl and other similar events often do not account for mitigating factors, such as the “substitution effect” of people who choose not to visit the Bay Area for business or tourism when major events are held here to avoid higher hotel prices and congestion, he said previously.
But for events like the World Cup, with multiple matches with days in between each, Noll said visitors would likely stay for longer and spend money here.
The boost from the World Cup was undeniable in downtown San José, where the San José Earthquakes hosted a watch party for all 104 matches over 39 days at San Pedro Square Market.
Closed streets and massive viewing screens, along with special permission from the city to allow outdoor drinking, drew thousands of people into the area for matches.
Mayor Matt Mahan’s office said the watch parties, activities and entertainment options in downtown brought 1 million cumulative visits to the area.
While most of the celebrations were peaceful, police reported some shootings and stabbings in the area following some of the events, and huge crowds forced organizers to relocate one viewing party to nearby Discovery Meadow to allow for more space. World Cup events were also canceled at Spark Social in San Francisco after a shooting in the Mission Bay neighborhood.
In June, the Bay Area Host Committee launched a Leadership Council and Corporate Membership Program in support of turning the committee into a “permanent, sustainable sports commission that will secure, support and celebrate major sporting events in the region for decades to come.”
The region is set to host the WNBA All-Star Game in 2027 at Chase Center, and the MLB All-Star Game will return to Oracle Park in 2028. Janmohamed said, with the coming events, “We will continue the incredible momentum of the past two years and directly increase positive economic impact for the Bay.”

articles.title_orig: What's gone wrong at Nike? How the world's sportswear giant lost its mojo
articles.title_zh: What's gone wrong at Nike? How the world's sportswear giant lost its mojo
articles.content_orig:
It's been a difficult few years for Nike.
The largest sportswear brand on the planet, named after the ancient Greek goddess of victory, has been losing of late. Losing sales, losing customers and losing ground to its rivals.
The one-time industry disruptor is now the establishment and in the middle of a tricky turnaround plan aimed at clinging on to market dominance.
Nike's latest financial results show signs a turnaround strategy put in place by company veteran Elliott Hill, who was coaxed out of retirement two years ago to lead the firm, is working - but the pace of change is more marathon than sprint.
However, its recovery has been dented by the loss of football star Kylian Mbappé, who ended his 20-year association with the brand last week to join fast-growing Swiss rival, On.
The Real Madrid striker's departure raises the question of whether Nike can remain the top logo for not just elite athletes, but also the fans that idolise them.
To be clear, Nike is still a mega brand and popular the world over. But missteps have seen hundreds of billions of dollars wiped off its stock market value as its share price tumbled by 75% over five years.
Last month, Nike was ejected from the S&P 100 stock market index of the biggest blue-chip firms in the US.
So what's gone wrong? And can Hill turn things around?
Matt Powell, a veteran analyst and adviser in the sports retail industry, reckons Nike has made "several strategic errors" which have been difficult to reverse, including cutting ties with retailers to sell only direct to customers online and making limited editions items more available.
"The more broadly available those shoes became, the fewer people were interested," Powell says.
Other self-inflicted wounds he suggests include spending research and development cash on digital operations rather than new products.
"They really shut down their innovation on product. Someone jokingly said they were trying to turn Nike into eBay."
That jibe was aimed at John Donahoe, the former eBay boss behind Nike's online direct-to-consumer sales pivot, before he made way for Hill.
Donahoe's four years at Nike coincided with the company's share price plunge.
His tenure saw sales initially soar, driven by pandemic restrictions that boosted online shopping, but subsequent cost-of-living pressures curbed customer spending.
As demand weakened overseas in key markets like China, Nike announced cost cuts and redundancies.
Its digital distraction allowed newer footwear firms on top of the trends to snap at its heels. Shop shelf space previously occupied by Nike was replaced by brands such as On and Hoka.
This was a stark warning to a company that prided and built itself on innovation.
Nike was the firm that signed a deal with a rookie called Michael Jordan in the mid-1980s at a time when the company wasn't a major player in basketball and still mostly known for its running trainers.
The gamble - spending its entire basketball budget on Jordan before he had even competed in the NBA - made Nike what it is today.
The company built a shoe brand around him - Air Jordan. The red and black colours broke NBA rules, but Nike used it as a marketing stunt and paid the fines.
In years that followed Nike partnered with generational talents Tiger Woods, Serena Williams and Cristiano Ronaldo, who all donned the Swoosh on their way to golf, tennis and football greatness.
While the brand retains partnerships with long-retired Jordan, plus Williams and Ronaldo - Woods ended his association in 2024 .
"[I'm] not saying that what they did wasn't great, but it was in the past," said Tim Derdenger, an academic in marketing and strategy. "It's not the future and it's not the current and that is what drives apparel sales today."
Nike's books still boast top athletes, ranging from Rory McIlory to Vinicius Junior.
However, it has now lost its biggest footballing star in Mbappé, who had been with Nike since he was nine years old, along with World Cup winner Lamine Yamal.
Yamal suggested his move to Adidas gave him the chance to stand out from Nike's star-studded roster, while Mbappé said On would see him "surrounded by innovators who dream of the same things I do".
Was that a parting dig at Nike?
Derdenger suggests Mbappé's move had parallels to Jordan's decision decades earlier to choose Nike over Converse and Adidas due to the opportunity for the athlete to become synonymous with one brand.
"Athletes have egos and those egos want them to be a part of something big and that they're the ones that are helping drive that change, that growth."
Nike boss Hill said the brand has had "some great moments" with Mbappé over two decades.
"We wish him much success as he makes the move," he said during Nike's earnings call, adding that the brand still has a "great stable of athletes".
For all the "doom and gloom", Nike will stay number one, according to Powell - millions worldwide, including young people, remain loyal - but its mistakes have dented its dominance.
"Will Nike be the gorilla they once were? I don't think so. Can the brand come back to growth and profitability? Yes," Powell says.
"When you shut down innovation, you don't turn it back on and it goes right back to full speed," he adds.
Powell thinks Nike's turnaround plan, called "Sport Offense", will start to show positive signs next year.
Hill said Nike had "more work to do" on its sportswear, Jordan brand and in China as the company announced quarterly revenues of $11bn (£8.3bn), which undershot analysts' expectations.
Notably, the company cited "headwinds" in China, where revenue declined by 26%.
Sales of its Jordan brand were also down globally. Hill said the firm had been "oversupplying" the iconic retro shoe and will now reduce the volume and frequency of products under the brand.
Nike said it expected revenues to decline by "high-single digits" in the financial year ahead, adding that it planned to make savings of $2.5bn by 2031, some of which will result in job losses.
Nike's chief financial officer Dave Denton said: "Our results are below both our expectations and our potential, and we are focused on closing this gap."
The company's shares fell by more than 8% in extended trading in New York after the earnings were announced.
Last year the company launched a spin-off campaign to its iconic "Just Do It" slogan aimed at younger generations with the line "Why Do It?"
Young people, and future sporting stars, may ask themselves: Why Nike?
Additional reporting by Osmond Chia

articles.title_orig: Global bond rout deepens, pushes US Treasury yields to 24-year peak
articles.title_zh: Global bond rout deepens, pushes US Treasury yields to 24-year peak
articles.content_orig:
Treasury yields fell on Thursday, giving back some of the recent gains that propelled longer-dated rates to levels not seen in decades.
The 10-year Treasury yield breached a level last seen in April 2002, before easing 5 basis points to 5.243%. The 10-year influences rates on mortgage and auto loans and credit card debt. The yield on the 30-year Treasury bond also hit its highest in 24 years before dropping more than 2 basis points to 5.613%.
Yields and prices move inversely. One basis point equals 0.01%.
Jeff Kilburg, CEO of KKM Financial, said he sees the 10-year yield pulling back to around 4.5%-4.75% if the U.S. and Iran can reach a deal to end the war. "If we're going to continue to stay in Iran, then that's going to be problematic for the 10-year yield."
Government borrowing costs around the world continued their relentless march upward on Thursday, continuing a monthslong trend as investors voted with their feet over a lack of political will to tackle fiscal deficits, while inflation remains stubbornly above target and leading central banks move to push interest rates higher.
Major economies face "persistently large deficits and rising interest expenses — challenges long associated with debt-distressed emerging market sovereigns," the Institute of International Finance said last week .
Japan's 10-year yield hit its highest level since the mid-1990s. Japan's debt has come under pressure from a weaker yen and rate hikes by the Bank of Japan .
The yield on the German 10-year bund, the benchmark for the euro area, topped 3.6%, the highest since 2008, before easing back. Elsewhere in Europe, the French 10-year surged 8 basis points to 4.925%, Italy's 10-year was up 10 basis points to 4.706%, while the U.K.'s 10-year yield increased 5 basis points to 5.483%.
"It's worth noting, but people get pretty worked up about those sorts of spreads regularly, so I don't think it's a crisis point necessarily, as far as Germany versus France or Italy," said Michael Schumacher, former managing director at Wells Fargo. "If you look at some countries that have very poor structural dynamics, like the UK, and I'd be concerned about that. People don't typically trade gilts versus bunds as much, but just as a barometer of, say, market concern, I think that's one to watch."
Bonds had been moving in lockstep with oil prices , which have been turbulent as the U.S.-Israel war with Iran obstructed crude exports from the Middle East. Crude oil prices were higher on Thursday , with international benchmark Brent crude futures back above $100 a barrel.
"We could see [bond] buyers come in effectively to take advantage of those yields, which would have the effect of causing them to go down, but also one of the things that has kept the volatility in those yields in the long end of the curve has been what's going on with oil, what's going on with inflation," Nomi Prins, founder of Prinsights Global, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Thursday.
But sovereign wealth funds and central banks, among the main long-term holders of Treasury debt, are unlikely to go along, Prins said.
"We could see movement ... in Treasury yields going down if oil prices go down significantly, if there's a resolution" in the Middle East, Prins added.

articles.title_orig: Chicago aldermen question World Business Chicago ads featuring Mayor Johnson
articles.title_zh: Chicago aldermen question World Business Chicago ads featuring Mayor Johnson
articles.content_orig:
Promoting Chicago or promoting the mayor? Aldermen held a hearing on Thursday on World Business Chicago ads, featuring Mayor Johnson. Though, critics say the videos look like campaign commercials.
CHICAGO - Chicago aldermen questioned whether promotional videos produced by World Business Chicago featuring Mayor Brandon Johnson amount to city marketing or political advertising during a hearing Thursday.
Representatives from World Business Chicago did not attend the hearing. Critics argued the videos resemble campaign commercials, while the organization said Johnson is an appropriate spokesperson for the city and that no public funds were used to produce the ads.
World Business Chicago is public and privately financed, so some of your tax dollars do go toward it.
"World Business Chicago is supposed to sell Chicago to the world," said Ald. Samantha Nugent of the 39th Ward. "City and state funding, taxpayer dollars go towards World Business Chicago and taxpayer dollars should not be spent on political advertising, and this appears to be a political advertisement, and that is why we wanted to bring World Business to Chicago to come in for a conversation.
World Business Chicago receives much of its funding from city and state grants. They say touting the economy and billions in investment is core to their mission.
The Source: The information in this report came from statements made during a Chicago City Council hearing, comments from World Business Chicago and Ald. Samantha Nugent, and publicly available information about the organization's funding and mission.

SpaceX's latest astronaut launch just set a new space record.
The company's Crew-13 mission for NASA arrived at the International Space Station (ISS) today (Oct. 1) at 7:05 p.m. EDT (2305 GMT), 7 hours and 55 minutes after it launched from Florida's Space Coast .
That's the fastest any American spacecraft has ever reached the orbiting lab, NASA officials said.
The previous record was 12 hours and 33 minutes, set in November 2024 by SpaceX's Dragon cargo capsule during the robotic CRS-31 resupply flight . The fastest that astronauts had made the trip in a U.S. vehicle was 14 hours and 43 minutes, which was achieved by the Crew-11 mission in August 2025.
"We got lucky this time," Julianna Scheiman, director of NASA science and Dragon programs at SpaceX , said during Crew-13's post-launch press conference today.
"The space station was in an opportune spot in space, and the orbital mechanics, the physics of it all, worked out for it to be the shortest launch-to-docking time we've had to date," she said, adding that "this is close to the fastest it could be."
Crew-13 didn't set the overall speed record to the ISS, however — not even close. In May 2020, a Russian Soyuz spacecraft carrying three astronauts reached the orbiting lab just 3 hours and 3 minutes after lifting off from Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan. The Soyuz caught up to the ISS after just two orbits of Earth.
The Soyuz isn't faster or more powerful than a cargo or crew-carrying Dragon capsule. Rather, the difference in chase-down times comes down primarily to choices made by mission controllers ; Russia tends to target more aggressive "fast-track" trajectories.
Crew-13 delivered four astronauts to the orbiting lab: NASA's Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, Joshua Kutryk of the Canadian Space Agency and Sergey Teteryatnikov of the Russian space agency Roscosmos . The quartet will live and work in space for the next six months.
They'll relieve the four astronauts of SpaceX's Crew-12 mission , which launched in mid-February. Those spaceflyers — NASA astronauts Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, the European Space Agency 's Sophie Adenot and cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev — could return to Earth in their Crew Dragon capsule as soon as Monday (Oct. 5), according to NASA officials.
Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

articles.title_orig: Judge denies motion asking for Lindsay Clancy to be found not guilty due to lack of evidence
articles.title_zh: Judge denies motion asking for Lindsay Clancy to be found not guilty due to lack of evidence
articles.content_orig:
A judge on Thursday denied Lindsay Clancy's request to be acquitted of murder charges in the deaths of her three young children.
Judge William Sullivan's decision came two days after Clancy returned to court for the first time since her murder trial ended with a deadlocked jury .
Defense attorney Kevin Reddington had asked Sullivan for an acquittal, arguing that prosecutors had not presented enough evidence to prove that Clancy carried out the killings.
The argument marked a shift from her trial defense, which did not dispute that she killed the children but maintained that she was not criminally responsible because of mental illness.
"This entire case is based on speculation," Reddington said. "Where is the admission? Where does she say that she did this?"
Prosecutor Shanan Buckingham called the argument "laughable."
"There was evidence introduced, both physical and circumstantial, that would permit a rational trier of fact to find beyond a reasonable doubt the elements of the charge of murder," Sullivan wrote in his ruling.
The next hearing in the case is set for Nov. 2.
During the trial, Clancy's attorneys did not dispute that she fatally strangled her children — Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and 8-month-old Callan — with exercise bands at their Duxbury, Mass., home in January 2023. She had been charged with three counts of murder in the first degree.
Her lawyers argued that she could not be held criminally responsible for the killings because she had the rare mental illness that they said made her unable to understand the wrongfulness of her actions.
Prosecutors contended that Clancy, who was never formally diagnosed with postpartum psychosis, carefully planned the killings and bears full responsibility for her children's deaths.
The trial hinged largely on discussions of Clancy's mental state. Over nearly five weeks of testimony, a series of family members and medical professionals took the stand to describe the mental and emotional struggles she endured in the months leading up to the killings.
During deliberations, the 12-member jury informed the judge that the panel was deadlocked: 11 members believed Clancy was not guilty, but one juror refused to apply the legal standard of reasonable doubt, preventing the jury from returning a unanimous not-guilty verdict.
The case finally ended on Sept. 4 following nearly 40 hours of deliberation after the jury came to the judge for a third time to inform him that they were deadlocked, triggering an automatic mistrial under Massachusetts law.
Advocacy groups and researchers said the mistrial highlighted how little the medical field knows about postpartum psychosis, a rare illness estimated to affect one to two per 1,000 women after delivery .
Clancy, who has been paralyzed from the waist down since she jumped from a second-story window after strangling her children, is expected to remain at a psychiatric hospital where she's been held for the last three years until her case is resolved.
Clancy's attorneys have also asked the judge to dismiss the case on the grounds that the holdout juror should have been removed.
Prosecutors have yet to decide whether to retry Clancy, Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz told reporters after the hearing. They could choose to retry her on first-degree murder charges, seek to try her on lesser charges, negotiate a plea deal or drop the case altogether.
"We are going to do what we can for the children," Cruz said. "That is what this case is about."

articles.title_orig: Judge says U.S. can’t prosecute ex-Olympian again in Reflecting Pool case
articles.title_zh: Judge says U.S. can’t prosecute ex-Olympian again in Reflecting Pool case
articles.content_orig:
Former Olympic canoeist David Hearn, left, and his attorney Norm Eisen, right, leave D.C. court with a smile in early September after a hearing about the dismissal of his vandalism charges. Mark Schiefelbein/AP hide caption
A judge has dismissed with prejudice the government's vandalism charges against former Olympic canoeist David Hearn. That means federal prosecutors cannot refile them in the future, despite President Trump's public demands to do so.
In fact, as D.C. Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman explained in a 26-page ruling released Thursday, the case should be permanently closed in large part because of the "political pressure brought by the President of the United States upon his subordinate officers."
"While the prosecutors admit that the evidence indicates that he committed no crime, the President's statements create a risk that Mr. Hearn will be prosecuted nonetheless, either because the current United States Attorney and her assistants will eventually yield to his public pressure campaign or because the President will replace them with prosecutors more likely to carry out his wishes," wrote Edelman, an Obama appointee.
Hearn, 67, was arrested at the Reflecting Pool in June, around the time its multimillion-dollar new blue lining started noticeably peeling off in chunks. He was charged with one felony count of property destruction and quickly indicted by a grand jury , though he pleaded not guilty .
In late July, however, with a trial start date — and the prospect of up to 10 years in prison if convicted — looming, Pirro's office abruptly asked the judge to drop the charges against Hearn and three others altogether.
Citing new reports from the Department of the Interior and National Park Service, federal prosecutors admitted that the Reflecting Pool damage was, in fact, "the result of botched installation and not vandalism."
Trump disagreed, and publicly urged Pirro to revisit the case — which Thursday's ruling prevents.
When asked for comment, the White House referred NPR to three of Trump's Truth Social posts from August, blaming the Reflecting Pool damage on vandals and disagreeing with U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro's decision to drop charges against Hearn in the first place.
Hearn's supporters rally outside the District of Columbia Courthouse during an early September hearing. Mark Schiefelbein/AP hide caption
Neither the U.S. Attorney's Office for D.C. nor the Department of Justice returned NPR's requests for comment in time for publication.
Hearn's lawyers — Norm Eisen, Mary Dohrmann, Steve Levin and Michael Bromwich — celebrated the ruling in a joint statement, calling it "a victory for the rule of law and for an innocent American seeking justice."
"This case never should have been brought in the first place," they said. "This was a miscarriage of justice, and what happened to Mr. Hearn is an outrage that should shock every American."
The soft-spoken Maryland resident quickly became a cause célèbre for the many Americans captivated by the Reflecting Pool saga , which some saw as a referendum on the Trump administration itself.
In an August interview with NPR , Hearn described his experience as "Kafkaesque" and "Orwellian," but said he was buoyed by the support he'd received from within and beyond his community.
"With the power of the law, the power of the courts, and my wonderful team, I feel very well equipped … to bring democracy back to me," he said.
Trump railed against Pirro in the days and weeks after she dropped the charges, saying she had "choked" and "folded like an umbrella" — and didn't rule out firing her. He continued to blame the damage on vandalism and wrote on social media that anyone who disagreed "should go back to Law School."
"Most concerningly," Edelman wrote, during that time, the president also leveled increasingly personal attacks against Hearn and his legal team.
"U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro should re-visit her hastily made decision, especially since it turned out that the 'gentleman' involved is a big player in ActBlue, a disgraceful fundraising SCAM, and is represented by a TRUMP DERANGED SLEAZEBAG, Political Hack Lawyer, Norm Eisen," Trump wrote in early August , in one of the social media posts the White House directed NPR to on Thursday.
It's against that backdrop that Hearn's legal team has been lobbying the judge to dismiss the charges with prejudice, to prevent the same case from being revived. The Trump administration, on the other hand, sought to leave that door open.
Edelman's Thursday ruling offers a peek into the government's argument — and then dismantles it.
The empty, fenced-off Reflecting Pool as seen in late September. Rod Lamkey/AP hide caption
Edelman wrote that when asked in court what kind of hypothetical new evidence might prompt prosecutors to revisit the case, an unnamed assistant U.S. attorney "waxed philosophical, musing, 'I don't know what the future may bring. None of us do.'"
He says prosecutors could not provide any specific examples of such evidence, and "admitted that the government was no longer even investigating the case."
"Given its own description of the existing evidence and the circumstances of this case, the development of contrary evidence seems practically inconceivable, and the possibility of a future meritorious prosecution strikes the Court as fanciful," Edelman concluded.
Hearn's lawyers say Thursday's ruling allows him "to move forward with his life as he deserves."
The Reflecting Pool, which was drained after July 4th, remains empty and fenced off for repairs, with no public timeline for completion.

articles.title_orig: Researchers using deer season to track spread of New World Screwworm
articles.title_zh: Researchers using deer season to track spread of New World Screwworm
articles.content_orig:
LUBBOCK, Texas (KCBD) - After New World Screwworm was confirmed in the U.S. nearly 80 years after its eradication, experts are hoping this year’s deer hunting season will help them track the spread.
The USDA reports there are two active cases in Texas - one in Crockett County, and the other in Presidio County.
Animals in those zones must be certified before they can be moved out of the region. A surveillance zone surrounds the infested area, where sterile flies are released as part of the response effort.
Dr. Sarabeth Hill, an assistant professor of veterinary practice in parasitology at the Texas Tech School of Veterinary Medicine, says while the spread is largely controlled, it’s harder to determine whether it’s impacting wildlife.
“I think with deer season, more people out there with eyes on animals we don’t always see, is going to be a really fantastic tool for us managing this infection,” Dr. Hill said.
While there haven’t been any reports of infections in deer so far, Texas Parks and Wildlife reports the previous outbreak in the 1950s and 60s resulted in the loss of between one third and one half of the Texas deer population.
“Deer season will certainly be a very helpful tool for us to get a good idea of the true movement of this parasite,” Hill said.
Hill said deer open themselves up to infection more during rutting season, when they are more prone to fighting.
“Just looking at that behavior and potential for wounds, there’s a chance for those screwworm flies to take root there,” Hill said.
The New World Screwworm is attracted to live tissue, so Dr. Hill says hunters do not have to worry about their deer becoming infected after they’re shot.
She does encourage hunters to look at their deer closely, though, during processing. She says the key signs of infection are open, foul smelling wounds.
“If we see it, it’s definitely something to report to Parks and Wildlife,” Hill said. “You can just Google ‘TPWD NWS’ and it will take you to their sighting and reporting page. If you suspect anything, we as the state of Texas would rather be safe than sorry.”
Dr. Hill also added that even if you do come across a deer with an active infection, it doesn’t necessarily mean the entire animal is a waste. She said the parasite stays in the same wound track and does not spread because it relies on oxygen.
“The nature of the screwworm is to dig into a muscle. I, personally, would discard the muscle that is affected. That open wound opens the door to secondary infection,” Hill said. “Personally, I would be okay with the rest of that deer.”
Dr. Hill said while New World Screwworm is a serious issue, state, federal, and local officials have worked hard to contain the spread.
“We have historic events to look back on and learn from that really prepared us well this year,” Hill said. “I do not think there is reason for panic. The big takeaway is: if you’re out in the field this season, and I hope lots of people are, just take an extra second to check over those animals and help us out in the effort of reducing the spread.”
Archery season for white-tail deer opens Saturday, Oct. 3 . Youth-only season opens Oct. 30, and general season opens Nov. 7.
“Deer season is a great thing, I certainly enjoy it,” Hill said.

articles.title_orig: Apple’s reportedly developing a smart home camera that doesn’t record video
articles.title_zh: Apple’s reportedly developing a smart home camera that doesn’t record video
articles.content_orig:
﻿With Apple rumored to launch a smart home hub next month, it could come with a privacy-protecting security camera too.
﻿With Apple rumored to launch a smart home hub next month, it could come with a privacy-protecting security camera too.
Apple’s rumored push into smart home tech could include a smart home security camera that only gives users text event descriptions instead of video footage. Mark Gurman said in the first episode of the Power On podcast that the camera will be part of “a new Apple smart home ecosystem,” alongside Apple’s rumored smart home hub :
They’re also building home security products, both first-party and third-party home security products. And the biggest thing is a program called J450. And this is an offshoot and a companion product to the J490 smart home display. And these are little cameras that you can put around your house. They have very low frame rate. It looks like a cylinder. It looks like a metal giant, you know, chapstick.
And what does that mean? No video recording. So it’s a sensor that cannot actually pull in real video footage. It’s analyzing your environment in your home and around your home simply using AI.
Gurman also mentions that the camera uses “a very similar technology” to what Apple’s reportedly developing for a pair of AirPods with cameras that leaked earlier this year .
Instead of using something like mmWave for presence sensing, using an image sensor with AI embedded that processes everything on-device, like these Sony IMX500 sensors , could work without passing images that would need to be stored and secured. Apple Home currently has a “Detect Activity” setting for HomeKit Secure Video cameras that stops video streaming and recording, but continues tracking motion, similar to what Gurman describes.
He goes on to add that the smart home camera will have facial recognition for things like detecting when someone enters a room, but, “You’re not getting anything but text descriptions. There’s nothing you can do with it. There’s no video recording.”

articles.title_orig: Student protests grip France as Prime Minister Lecornu calls crisis meeting
articles.title_zh: Student protests grip France as Prime Minister Lecornu calls crisis meeting
articles.content_orig:
Hundreds of schools in France are closed as students continue to protest about a lack of teachers, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings
The protests started earlier this week in France's capital Paris before spreading across the country
Education minister Edouard Geffray tells French media that 65 school staff have been injured, including 40 headteachers
He adds that 1,949 people were arrested on Thursday alone
Some of the violence and damage has been truly shocking, with teenagers suffering eye injuries and one losing his teeth, writes our digital Europe editor
University students have also joined the demonstrations, citing similar concerns and demands
Edited by Jenna Moon and Sam Hancock, with Hugh Schofield reporting from Paris
These are some of the latest pictures coming in to us from across France, where disorder is continuing, sparked by a wave of student protests against conditions in schools.
In Paris, emergency personnel have been working to put out fires, while police in Brest are deploying tear gas on some demonstrators.
A protester throws a stop sign into a fire near Kerichen High School in Brest, western France
Police have used tear gas against protesters in Brest
The charred entrance to Roger Verlomme secondary school in Paris this morning
Firefighters put out a blaze outside Leonard de Vinci secondary school in Paris
French Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin has said there is an "active and violent minority" taking part in the protests.
"We're not entirely sure that they are even high school students themselves," he tells France's RTL radio. He adds that two-thirds of the 2,000 people arrested since protests began have been placed in police custody.
"We have gone from high-school student demonstrations to a public order disturbance. When people target buses and set schools on fire, it is no longer simply a protest issue," he adds.
The entrance hall at Nelson Mandela High School in Nantes was destroyed in a fire
French Education Minister Ãdouard Geffray says "more than a hundred" schools have experienced "severe damage" since the beginning of the protests.
He tells French broadcaster BFMTV that 65 staff members were injured, including 40 head teachers, and that 1,207 high schools were disrupted or blocked on Thursday.
Geffray adds that 160 students had to be evacuated by staff at Nelson Mandela high school in Nantes, western France.
The education minister argues that the student protests movement had been "hijacked" and that teachers had told him that "the people in front of me were not my students".
Ryad Rani, president of the USL union for secondary schools in France
Though protests first broke out in schools around Paris last month, the demonstrations spread nationwide after France's main union for secondary school students called for a nationwide blockade.
Union Syndicale LycÃ©enne (USL) called for the school blockade last week because, it said, "other student actions, such as petitions or demonstrations, elicit no response from our political leaders".
This blockade, which took place on Tuesday, was organised to coincide with a wider public sector strike against spending cuts in the government's draft budget.
With teachers among those striking on Tuesday, education union FÃ©dÃ©ration Syndicale Unitaire (FSU) backed the movement and called for the "fight for public services and education to become a collective struggle" in a statement on Thursday.
But the protests have also become a site for party political sparring, with the government and hard-right politicians blaming the hard left - in particular the radical La France Insoumise (LFI) party - for igniting the protests. LFI's leader said blaming the left would not solve issues underlying the demonstrations.
Paul Kirby Europe digital editor
An increasing number of students, teachers and police have been injured in days of protests
Not enough teachers, overcrowded classrooms, a shortage of chairs and dilapidated school buildings - the grievances of Franceâs lycÃ©e students are real, and backed up by their teachers.
Education Minister Ãdouard Geffray conceded at the start that some of the studentsâ demands were "legitimate". One teacher in the Gironde summed it up by saying "their demands are the same as ours".
But some of the violence and damage over the past few days has been truly shocking.
Teenagers have suffered eye injuries, and one has lost his teeth as police with riot weapons tackle protests largely involving teenagers.
Police too have been injured, as have dozens of headteachers.
One teacher in Angers was seriously injured when he was struck on the head with an iron bar - his attackers were apparently not from the  school.
The question has now become how to stop "unbridled violence" as much as deal with high-school shortages. The crisis is also deeply political, with presidential elections only months away, and that makes the government's task that much harder.
More than 400 schools across France have been shut as the French government says student protests have descended into "urban violence".
Sixty-five staff members have been injured in the unrest and there has been "significant damage" to school facilities, with classes now taking place remotely, French education minister Ãdouard Geffray has said.
Student protests have broken out over a lack of teachers and staff, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings. University students also joined demonstrations on Thursday. The French interior ministry says 1,949 people were arrested, with 305 police officers injured.
The blockades and protests at French lycÃ©es - for 15 to 18-year-old students - began last week before spreading to hundreds of schools across the country.
So far, 1,027 lycÃ©es have been affected by demonstrations, with blockades at 222 of them, according to the interior ministry.
At least 30 universities have also reportedly been blockaded, including campuses in Rennes and Paris.
We'll be following developments throughout the day - stay with us.

articles.title_orig: Putin warns Russia is prepared to use ‘all weapons,’ including nuclear, to protect Kaliningrad
articles.title_zh: Putin warns Russia is prepared to use ‘all weapons,’ including nuclear, to protect Kaliningrad
articles.content_orig:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has warned the West against escalating the war in Ukraine , saying Moscow is prepared to use “all weapons” in its arsenal — including nuclear — if its Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad comes under attack.
Speaking at the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow on Thursday, the Russian leader said he had no plans to attack any European country but was prepared to respond to Western aggression if necessary and referenced the Russian territory sandwiched between NATO members Poland and Lithuania.
His warning follows recent military drills by NATO near Kaliningrad that the bloc has described as defensive exercises to strengthen deterrence. Those exercises have prompted strong concerns from Moscow, which warned in late September it would retaliate if NATO attempted to blockade the exclave by air or sea.
“The drills in the Baltic Sea, following one another … Then the attempts to arrest our ships and vessels. All this is an escalation. And then we began to hear statements regarding the Kaliningrad region,” Putin said.
“If it comes to direct attack against the Russian Federation, in this case on Kaliningrad and possibly some other territories, of course the issue of using all weapons in our country’s arsenal will inevitably and unavoidably emerge on the agenda. This is unavoidable,” he cautioned.
NATO, several European countries and the United Kingdom have accused Russia of conducting hybrid warfare against them, including cyberattacks, sabotage and espionage attempts, aimed at breaking their support for Ukraine.
Russia’s war in Ukraine, dubbed by Moscow as a “special military operation,” is now in its fifth year, but Putin shows no sign of slowing his offensive and has instead intensified strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and its capital city of Kyiv ahead of an anticipated bitterly cold winter.
But recent Ukrainian drone strikes on Russia’s oil refineries have led to widespread fuel shortages, shattering the illusion that the consequences of the conflict are far removed from ordinary Russians.
Long queues of cars at fuel stations have been seen in major cities, while hits on Russia’s largest online retailers have increased pressure on the already strained wartime economy.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky regularly refers to Ukrainian drone strikes deep inside Russian territory as “long-range sanctions,” designed to reduce Russia’s revenues, military capacity and push the Kremlin into negotiations.
In his speech Thursday to foreign policy and international affairs academics, Putin admitted the Ukrainian strikes were taking a toll on Russia’s economy, saying they had cost Russia 1% of its gross domestic product (GDP) and that Ukrainian military maneuvers in the Black Sea have taken out over 100 Russian ships.
However, Putin also made clear he remains undeterred.
“In the Black Sea — that’s a combat zone; we struck military vessels and ships transporting military cargo, and we hardly ever made a mistake. Throughout this whole saga, they [Ukraine] have knocked out over 100 of our ships. Well, we started hitting back, and now we’re being bombarded from every direction with appeals: “Oh, please stop doing that,” Putin said.
“It’s the same story with our oil refineries; they (Ukraine) openly declared their goal was to damage our economy. Did they succeed? Partially — by our estimates, we lost about one percent of our GDP. And it was done deliberately — these are civilian targets, after all. Well, they got a mirror-image response,” Putin added, sidestepping that it was Moscow who launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Putin’s admission of the economic toll comes just one day after he told newly elected members of the State Duma — the lower house of Russia’s parliament, which predictably saw the United Russia party that backs Putin hold onto its majority — that the Russian economy was stable.
Taking the opportunity to swipe at Ukraine, the Russian president on Wednesday derided Kyiv’s reliance on financial assistance from its Western allies.
Ruling pro-Putin party set to win Russia’s tightly controlled wartime parliamentary election
“Mistakes, especially now, are absolutely unacceptable,” he warned parliamentarians. “Unlike some, and we won’t point fingers, Russia can’t run around the world humiliating (itself) by begging for handouts with an outstretched hand,” he said.
“Firstly, because, as I have already said, it is humiliating. Secondly, no one is going to give us anything, and we know that very well. And thirdly, and most importantly, we do not need it. Russia’s financial system and economy are secure,” he continued.
While signaling in recent weeks that he does not intend to draw back from the war in Ukraine, Putin also said he would prefer the conflict to end through talks.
Ahead of the election, Putin had said the results would show Russians are united by the military and its goals — though the Levada Center, an independent pollster, found in an August poll that 59% of Russians favored moving to peace talks.
In a further sign that Putin does not plan to slow down the “special military operation,” budget documents reviewed by Reuters show that Russia plans to spend 17.1 trillion rubles ($205.112 billion) on defense in 2027, about 27% more than originally budgeted and the highest level since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI alerts more than 100 groups about rogue AI agent activity
articles.title_zh: OpenAI alerts more than 100 groups about rogue AI agent activity
articles.content_orig:
A legal nonprofit sued OpenAI in a California court on Tuesday over the company’s agents escaping a testing environment and hacking the open source AI platform Hugging Face . “OpenAI’s actions straightforwardly violated California law,” the suit alleges.
The suit was filed by Legal Advocates for Safe Science and Technology (LASST) and the law firm Gerstein Harrow in California Superior Court in San Francisco, where OpenAI is headquartered. It alleges that OpenAI’s agents violated California’s Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act (CDAFA) by breaching Hugging Face over the summer. The suit, which comes amid ongoing disclosures across the industry of agents going rogue, claims that OpenAI should be held responsible for the activity given a California AI law in effect since January 1 that says “it shall not be a defense … that the artificial intelligence autonomously caused the harm to the plaintiff.”
“We think it’s extremely important that existing laws are enforced to hold AI companies accountable for the harm they’re causing,” Tyler Whitmer, founder of LASST, tells WIRED. “Especially when that harm is caused by autonomous agents, because we see that as an obvious, extremely risky thing in the world that’s very new.”
“Hugging Face was a serious incident and we've taken a series of actions in response, but this lawsuit is completely without merit,” OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri told WIRED in a statement.
On Monday, Florida attorney general James Uthmeier filed for a temporary injunction against OpenAI to block development of models without independent oversight, amid a lawsuit Florida brought in June against OpenAI and its CEO, Sam Altman. OpenAI “asked the government to tie them to the mast. Well, Florida is answering their cries for help,” Uthmeier said in a statement.
Given that the whole point of AI agents is that they can be empowered to take actions on a (human) user’s behalf, AI developers and safety researchers have long foreseen that unintended “agentic” activity would be a concern as machine learning development progressed. Protections built into mainstream, consumer AI systems have largely prevented mass rogue activity so far, but rapidly advancing capabilities in general, as well as situations where guardrails are suspended (such as in the Hugging Face case where OpenAI had removed some model restraints for testing), have led to an apparent uptick in rogue agent activity.
As governments weigh AI regulation amid both existential safety questions and economic and national security considerations, researchers and people around the world have increasingly called for accountability mechanisms for AI. And from a legal perspective , experts have largely emphasized that questions of responsibility, liability, and culpability can only be answered through precedent set by cases working their way through courts.
“After the Hugging Face incident was disclosed, we actually did a bunch of work trying to educate regulators and civil society organizations about the hack. And we were kind of wondering, is anyone going to do anything about this in court?” Whitmer says. “There are structural reasons why we think Hugging Face, which is the obvious potential plaintiff to do something here, is not doing anything. So given that it didn’t seem like anyone else was going to do anything about this, we moved forward. As these systems scale and as things get crazier, AI really could be catastrophically harmful.”
LASST and Gerstein Harrow brought the lawsuit under California’s Unfair Competition Law, which requires that LASST allege both how its work and resources were impacted and diverted as a result of the Hugging Face incident, as well as unlawful activity by OpenAI.
The suit does not seek financial damages, and instead asks the court for injunctive relief such that OpenAI would be barred from developing AI agents that can autonomously hack other entities, plus legal fees and “any other relief deemed just and proper.”

articles.title_orig: Man Charged With Threatening Katie Miller, Wife of Top Trump Aide Stephen Miller
articles.title_zh: Man Charged With Threatening Katie Miller, Wife of Top Trump Aide Stephen Miller
articles.content_orig:
The FBI on Thursday arrested a man on a charge of stalking former Trump administration adviser Katie Miller, an administration official familiar with the investigation told NBC News.
John Anthony Proia III, 41, was arrested and charged with stalking over allegations that he called, texted and left voicemails with “disturbing messages” about the victim, who was described as a former political adviser, and her husband, who is currently a high-level federal government employee, the Justice Department said in a news release.
The Justice Department did not name Katie Miller, though an administration official familiar with the investigation confirmed to NBC News that the victim is Miller, who is married to White House deputy chief of staff for policy Stephen Miller and hosts a popular conservative podcast.
“Thank you Todd Blanche, Leah Foley, and the FBI Washington Field Office for keeping me and my family safe. Good to see a Boston grand jury indict this man,” Miller wrote in a post on X on Thursday, referring to Attorney General Todd Blanche and U.S. Attorney Leah Foley.
Proia was indicted by a federal grand jury in Boston on Thursday on one count of cyberstalking after being arrested earlier in the day. He allegedly contacted the former political adviser more than 40 times over the course of less than two months, according to the Justice Department.
The defendant also allegedly sent disturbing messages to Miller’s parents during the August 2026 to September 2026 time frame cited in court documents.
“As alleged in the Indictment, the defendant repeatedly and relentlessly targeted the victim, her husband and her family with deeply disturbing communications that profoundly disrupted their lives,” Foley said in a statement.
Ted Docks, special agent in charge of the FBI’s Boston Division, wrote in a statement on Thursday that Proia was arrested “for allegedly engaging in a sustained campaign of harassment to frighten this victim and her family, inflicting significant emotional distress.”
Proia made the calls, sent text messages and left voicemails from “an ever-changing series of unfamiliar phone numbers” to Miller, who lives in the Washington, D.C., area, the DOJ said.
The department added that those phone numbers were obtained through applications that provide free phone numbers for calling and messaging via Voice over Internet Protocol. The applications allow a user to hide their identity and easily generate new phone numbers, according to court filings.
According to court documents, Miller sometimes received multiple communications from Proia in one day, including calls made late at night. Miller did answer some of the calls, but Proia also left voicemails, the DOJ said.
The calls “were allegedly made by what appeared to be a male caller employing a menacing tone and often using expletives,” the Justice Department said.
The Justice Department also detailed some text messages sent to phone numbers associated with Miller’s parents.
In one message, Proia allegedly wrote to Miller’s mother, calling Stephen Miller “evil” and Katie Miller a “creature.” Another message allegedly featured a photo of Katie Miller, while another read, “My god, how can you be proud of this filth?”
In a text message to the victim’s father, Proia allegedly wrote, “Hey [first name of victim’s father], how goes it? Hope your daughter marrying a Jewish Nazi/white supremacist is working out for you and [first name of victim’s mother]. Did you raise her to be trash or did that just happen naturally?”
Proia’s arrest comes after Bloomberg reported over the weekend that two senior FBI officials in Washington were demoted and reassigned to FBI headquarters due to concerns that the agency was not moving efficiently enough to investigate threatening phone calls made to Miller, three people familiar with the matter told Bloomberg.
Darren Cox, the agency’s Washington Field Office’s assistant director in charge, said in a statement to Bloomberg that the move was a personnel decision made at the field office level based on “our constant evaluation of mission needs.”
Michael Kosnar is the Justice Department Producer for NBC News.
Kyla Guilfoil is a breaking news reporter on the politics team for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Discovery of Exquisite Feathered Dinosaur in China Could Rewrite The Evolution of Flight
articles.title_zh: Discovery of Exquisite Feathered Dinosaur in China Could Rewrite The Evolution of Flight
articles.content_orig:
An exquisitely preserved feathered raptor just discovered in north-eastern China could probably fly.
It's also somewhat disrupted the evolutionary path we thought birds took to get into the air.
Norellraptor barsboldi, as the new dinosaur has been named, is a microraptor, which means it's a small dinosaur with feathers and wings.
It's also a member of the wider group Paraves , which includes a range of theropod dinosaurs , including some that are still thriving today: birds.
And, like its living relatives, Norellraptor could probably fly.
But close analysis of this remarkably detailed fossil suggests the evolutionary path to flight may be far more forked than we thought.
Norellraptor is described in a new paper by paleontologist Xuri Wang of the Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences and his colleagues. The paper is published in Nature Communications .
The microraptor's body is 57 centimeters long (just over 22 inches), and based on its bones, the researchers think it hadn't quite finished growing at the time of its death.
Its feathers are much less well-preserved than its bones, but from what the researchers could see, its forelimbs and tail seem to have been festooned with flight-related plumage, while other parts of its body were covered in straight, simple feathers.
Certain features in this Norellraptor's bones, and a close look at where it sits in the Paraves family tree has led the researchers to question what we know about how flight evolved within Paraves.
The fact that both microraptors and birds evolved the ability to fly doesn't necessarily mean they inherited the trait from the same ancestor.
Norellraptor 's current position in the Paraves family tree suggests flight may have actually arisen at least twice, independently.
The steps it followed to reach the skies seem to be quite different from those taken by birds.
Another bit of evidence is that the development of the dinosaur's forearm, or wing, seems to have stopped quite early in its life, which is the opposite of what we see in modern, flying birds.
"The sequences of flight-related novelties reconstructed along the two lineages differ consistently," Wang and team write .
"Combined with histological evidence which might indicate a peculiar limb growth model in Microraptorinae, these results dismiss a shared developmental pattern driving the evolution of the flying dinosaurs and support multiple and independent selective regimes at the origin of the winged taxa in Paraves."
In other words, there might have been some convergent evolution going on in the Paraves family.
That's when two separate evolutionary groups reach a similar outcome via a totally different route. Think whales and fishes: both can swim using fins, but they arrived at that body plan from totally different paths.
Still, paleontologists can't rely on just one fossil to rewrite evolutionary history.
A lot more evidence will be needed before scientists are convinced that birds and microraptors did indeed evolve flight entirely independently.
"Microraptorines have been advocated as models for investigating the origin and evolution of the avian flight," the authors note .
"Yet, the evolutionary relationships between the flight apparatus of birds and the purported aerial adaptations of the microraptorines are controversial from both functional and phylogenetic perspectives."
The research has been published in Nature Communications .

articles.title_orig: New details released after death of Chad Lowe's teenage daughter
articles.title_zh: New details released after death of Chad Lowe's teenage daughter
articles.content_orig:
By JUSTIN ENRIQUEZ, US ASSISTANT SHOWBIZ EDITOR and SONIA HORON, US ASSISTANT SHOWBIZ EDITOR and BRIAN MARKS, US ASSISTANT SHOWBUSINESS EDITOR
Published: 19:28 EDT, 1 October 2026 | Updated: 21:34 EDT, 1 October 2026
Chad Lowe's 13-year-old daughter died by suicide, the County of Los Angeles Medical Examiner has concluded.
Emergency services responded to the family home at 12.10am on Tuesday and the teen was transported to an area hospital where the Medical Examiner said she was pronounced dead at 1.14am.
The autopsy report also reveals that her body may now be released to her parents.
The Lowes announced the news of Fiona's death in a statement on Tuesday, describing their devastation at the loss of 'a loving young girl who was smart, creative and loved to dance.'
'She was adored by her sisters and she was deeply loved by her parents,' the statement continued. 'In fact, she was the light of our lives.'
The family also urged anyone struggling with mental health to reach out to the suicide prevention helpline.
Chad Lowe's daughter Fiona, 13, died by suicide, the County of Los Angeles Medical Examiner concluded on Thursday, adding that she passed away in hospital at 1.14am on Tuesday
The Lowes' statement on Tuesday confirming Fiona's death described her as 'the light of our lives' and added: 'She was adored by her sisters and she was deeply loved by her parents'
The actor shared Fiona with wife Kim Painter. The couple are also parents to daughters Mabel, 17, and Nixie, ten
Fiona was the middle child of Lowe and wife Kim Painter who married in 2010. They also share daughters Mabel, 17, and Nixie, ten.
Her grandfather Charles Lowe, the father of Chad and his older brother and fellow actor Rob, shared a touching tribute to her on Wednesday.
He posted a heartwarming photo of Fiona smiling at the camera as she swam in a pool, writing: 'Rest in peace sweet Fiona.'
Parents at the teen's school received an email from the principal on Tuesday, letting them know that a student had died, according to Page Six. The email did not specify who it was.
The message offered condolences to the student's family and advised that 'counselors are available to meet with students and staff who may need emotional support during this difficult time.'
'Her passing is devastating for our entire family,' Tuesday's statement said, while directing anyone struggling with mental health to reach out to the suicide prevention helpline
Lowe's father, Charles Lowe, shared a touching tribute to his granddaughter Fiona on Wednesday sharing a sweet photo of her swimming in a pool
Charles is also father to Chad's older brother and fellow actor Rob Lowe, seen together at the 2002 Emmy Awards in Los Angeles
Lowe's Instagram account is full of heartwarming photos of his three daughters.
The doting dad paid tribute to Fiona last November on her birthday, sharing a photo of her beaming in cowboy boots.
'Celebrating Fiona officially becoming a teen today!!' the Emmy winner wrote. 'Keep dancing through life FiBear! Love you soooo much!!'
The actor also shared a photo of all three of his daughters in February 2025, showing them visiting the ruins of their childhood home in Los Angeles, following the devastating Palisades wildfire.
The girls were seen with their arms around each other as they looked on at the ruins.
'Almost a month after we evacuated our girls finally got to go back to see what's left of their home,' he wrote in the caption.
'The way they’ve handled this whole devastating experience is nothing short of remarkable. I am in awe of their spirit and resilience. Helping them navigate these tough times is my sole purpose. Being their dad is my life’s greatest joy and privilege.'
'However, this terrible experience has been a powerful reminder of this simple truth - we can't always control what happens to us in this life but we can control how we respond. And I have been so incredibly proud of how my wife Kim and our daughters have strived to make the absolute best of this extraordinarily difficult circumstance. I am in awe of their resilience.'
Lowe, who has appeared on TV shows such as ER, 24, Melrose Place and Now And Again, reflected on being a 'girl dad' on the Still Here Hollywood podcast in August 2024
'Having daughters is such an incredible privilege,' he shared on the podcast. 'And so I look at the world, really, from their perspective'
Lowe, who has appeared on TV shows such as ER, 24, Melrose Place and Now And Again, reflected on being a 'girl dad' on the Still Here Hollywood podcast in August 2024.
'Having daughters is such an incredible privilege,' he shared.
'It takes what I've known intellectually about women and all of equality and the glass ceiling that's there, and how it's a misogynistic world in a lot of ways... And it's put it in my heart, because I have three daughters. And so I look at the world, really, from their perspective.'
The proud dad also raved about taking his three girls to Taylor Swift's concert in 2023, sharing sweet snaps on Instagram and writing, 'It’s official, I’m a certified Swiftie Dad! I totally get it now! What an awesome night!'
Lowe married Painter following the end of his first marriage to actress Hilary Swank, which lasted 10 years and ended in divorce in 2007.
He won an Emmy Award in 1993 for his supporting role on the comedy-drama series Life Goes On, where he starred as a man living with HIV.
If you or someone you know needs help, please call or text the confidential 24/7 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline in the US on 988. There is also an online chat available at 988lifeline.org

articles.title_orig: Thieves smash into Fayetteville's Hawley's Bicycle World, steal $5K in bikes
articles.title_zh: Thieves smash into Fayetteville's Hawley's Bicycle World, steal $5K in bikes
articles.content_orig:
FAYETTEVILLE, NC (WTVD) -- Hawley's Bicycle World, a community staple on Raeford Road for more than 60 years, is picking up the pieces after a break-in early Tuesday morning that left the shop boarded up and its owners uneasy.
Surveillance cameras captured the moment three masked suspects smashed through a window at the longtime local business, making off with three bicycles, including two high-end e-bikes, within a minute.
The thieves remain at large.
"It's very disappointing, I guess, because you do try so hard to do everything right. We have cameras. We have alarm systems," said Sandy Hawley, co-owner of Hawley's Bicycle World. "We've had for two days now people coming in and trying to beef up the alarm system and figure out what could we have done to have stopped it in a way."
According to Fayetteville police, the suspects appear to be young people.
Hawley described what she saw in the footage: "To me, it looked like two of the gentlemen who came in are boys, just picked the first two bikes they could get. The third one looked like he was eyeballing one because it was a little further down in the display area and he went straight for that one and went out."
The break-in occurred around 1:50 a.m. on September 29.
Officers arrived to find a window smashed by what police described as an "unknown means." The suspects took one orange Velotric Tempo electric bicycle, one glacier mint Aventon electric bicycle, and one black Giant Roam mountain bike, with the combined value of the stolen bikes estimated at $5,000, not including the cost to repair the window.
Hawley detailed how the thieves entered the shop, "They came onto the property and scoped a little bit, then started looking for how they could get into the building. They went behind us, found a rock or stone or concrete, and used that to bust through the window. It took him several times."
For the Hawley family, the crime feels deeply personal.
"When you've been involved in somebody and take something that belongs to you, it becomes really personal and you feel violated. So, it just takes you back to the all those places and triggers again," Hawley said.
Hawley's Bicycle World first opened in 1964, when Hawley's father-in-law, a veteran, began by selling tent campers and lawnmowers.
Over the decades, the shop has grown into a gathering place for local cyclists and families.
Long-time customer and bike club member Reita Los said, "They'll give you a discount and they take care of you. They help you out and it's just a great store." She added, "I mean, it just made me sad that Fayetteville would do this to someone that's been here forever."
Despite the setback, Hawley says the outpouring of support from the community has been heartening.
"We are as a family, very humbled by everyone who has already reached out to us just from seeing some video that was posted on social media and sharing it. "
The family plans to increase security measures, adding more alarms to the 32 cameras already in place.
Hawley urges anyone with information to come forward. Anyone with information is asked to contact Detective C. Melvin at (472) 242-8287.
